screening_notes: Criteria 1-5 are met: DL is the primary method, 3D CT volumes processed (hybrid 2D+3D branch), liver is segmented (plus tumor) from CT (LiTS + private scans), Dice global 96.2% reported. However, the method section describes a re-implementation of H-DenseUNet (Li et al. 2017, ref [46]) with Han's ResNet-based liver localization (ref [45]): the pipeline (ResNet ROI, 2D Dense-UNet + 3D Dense-UNet, feature fusion layer) is cited directly to these prior works rather than presented as modified. The only additions are standard histogram equalization preprocessing and morphological postprocessing — no new architecture, loss, training scheme, ablation, or comparison table is presented, and the single 96.2% global Dice on a mixed 35-scan test set is not shown to improve on the original H-DenseUNet results. The genuine contribution is the surgical-applicability discussion, which is not a methodological contribution under the inclusion criteria. Borderline call: a lenient reading of 'hybrid network' as the authors' contribution would flip this to INCLUDE.
exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution (Exclusion criterion 7)

title: Automatic Segmentation of Kidney and Renal Tumor in CT Images Based on 3D Fully Convolutional Neural Network with Pyramid Pooling Module
architecture: 3D_FCN_PPM (3D Fully Convolutional Network with Pyramid Pooling Module)
architecture_details: 13 residual blocks (39 conv layers) from ResNet, only 2 pooling layers to preserve detail, dilated convolutions for larger receptive field, 4-branch PPM with pooling/deconv kernel sizes 2/4/8/16, end-to-end on 3D volumes (64-slice sub-volumes)
loss_function: Weighted cross entropy (class weights: kidney 1.0, tumor 2.0, background 0.2)
preprocessing: ROI cropping (150x150 window) via coarse multi-atlas segmentation from prior work [4]; CT value clamping to [-200HU, 500HU]; normalization to 0-1 and mean subtraction; data augmentation (flipping, random cropping focused on kidney/tumor region, ~90,000 training images)
postprocessing: Sub-volume result concatenation with majority voting on overlaps; 3D conditional random field; connected component analysis with 18-connectivity keeping largest kidney/tumor component
datasets: ["In-house CT angiography dataset (First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University)"]
dataset_size: 140 patients; 90 ROIs (lesioned kidney) training, 50 ROIs testing, one ROI per patient
comparison_methods: ["2D_PSPNet", "3D_UNet"]
limitations: GPU memory limits input to 64 slices, forcing sub-volume splitting; under-segmentation of small tumors (lowest tumor Dice 0.440 on ~6ml tumor); biased prediction near renal hilum; difficulty assembling large annotated datasets for training
future_work: Network described as general and extendable to other applications; authors highlight the need for large datasets with ground truth

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) DL primary method — FCN with bi-directional ConvLSTM sequential feature extractors; (2) 3D volumetric context — processes 7-slice chunks and models inter-slice relations via ConvLSTM (not slice-independent 2D, so exclusion #3 does not apply; note: uses 2D convs + RNN, not 3D convolutions, hence is_3d=false per schema definition); (3) segments liver, spleen, gallbladder; (4) CT (LiTS challenge); (5) reports Dice with std, per-case analysis, FP ratios; (6) novel architecture (sequential feature extractor). Study type: method — novel segmentation architecture, not a framework/tooling, review, or dataset paper.
title: SequentialSegNet: Combination with Sequential Feature for Multi-organ Segmentation
architecture: SequentialSegNet (SSN): U-Net-style FCN with bi-directional ConvLSTM sequential feature extractors on skip connections
architecture_details: 5-level encoder-decoder FCN; 4 sequential feature extractors (forward + backward ConvLSTM) connecting contracting and expanding paths on top 4 levels; CT volume fed as overlapping chunks of 7 consecutive slices; multi-class softmax replaces binary classifier; 2D convolutions (kernel 3) with 2D max-pooling/deconvolution — inter-slice context captured via ConvLSTM rather than 3D convolutions
loss_function: Weighted pixel-wise cross-entropy (class weights: background 1, liver 3, spleen 3, gallbladder 5)
preprocessing: Orientation normalization (rotation/flip so liver and backbone positioned left/bottom across sources); HU clipping to [-75, 175]
postprocessing: None mentioned
datasets: ["MICCAI 2017 LiTS Challenge training set (with manually annotated spleen and gallbladder verified by a radiologist)"]
dataset_size: 131 CT volumes (110 used for 3-organ experiments; 21 cases lacked gallbladder due to cholecystectomy/other reasons)
dice_per_organ: {"liver": 95.91, "spleen": 91.3, "gallbladder": 75.57, "note": "4-fold cross-validation, multi-organ SSN, per-case Dice % (Table II); main 83/27 split gave liver 95.58, spleen 91.41, gallbladder 74.72 (Table I)"}
other_metrics: {"std_dev_dice": {"liver": 3.28, "spleen": 7.28, "gallbladder": 16.57}, "gallbladder_extirpation_fp_analysis": "On all-131-case set: SSN FP ratio 80.95% vs U-net 90.48%; SSN shows 9.88% less gallbladder Dice drop than U-net in extirpation scenario", "inference_time_seconds_per_volume": "2.39 minutes"}
comparison_methods: ["U-net (2D, single-organ and multi-organ variants)", "Roth et al. hierarchical 3D FCN [25] (competitive Dice; SSN inference ~half the time)", "Single-organ vs multi-organ ablations"]
limitations: Gallbladder extirpation in ~16.03% of cases causes false positives and dramatically lowers Dice (Dice = 0% when organ segmented in extirpated case); challenging cases include hepatic adipose infiltration, CT artifacts, liver lesions, and cholelithiasis; gallbladder Dice has high variance (std up to ~32% in extirpation-inclusive evaluation)
future_work: Design efficient measures to handle false positives in organ-extirpation scenarios; potentially introduce an organ detection stage before segmentation so the model knows which organs to segment

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) deep learning is primary method (FCN with SharpMask-style feature fusion + CRFasRNN); (2) operates on volumetric thoracic CT scans with voxel-wise loss, 3D B-spline deformation augmentation, and volume-level Dice; convolution dimensionality is not explicitly stated (7x7 kernels may indicate 2D per-slice convs), which is the only minor ambiguity — the overall pipeline has 3D context, so exclusion criterion 3 does not apply; (3) segments 4 thoracic organs at risk (esophagus, heart, trachea, aorta); (4) CT modality; (5) quantitative Dice ratio with std and paired t-tests; (6) novel contribution (transposed-conv refinement module replacing bilinear upsampling, channel-aligned fusion, end-to-end trainable CRFasRNN with learnable compatibility function). title: Segmentation of Organs at Risk in Thoracic CT Images Using a SharpMask Architecture and Conditional Random Fields
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI 2017)
architecture: FCN with SharpMask feature-fusion refinement + CRF as RNN (CRFasRNN)
architecture_details: 10-layer FCN: 5 conv+ReLU+max-pool layers followed by 5 transposed-conv+ReLU layers; 7x7 kernels; 5 output channels (4 organs + background); SharpMask-style top-down refinement using conv+ReLU (instead of copying feature maps) to match channel counts, with transposed convolutions replacing bilinear upsampling; CRFasRNN module on top with learnable kernel weights (omega) and compatibility function (mu), trained end-to-end via BPTT; trained with SGD (lr 0.1, x0.1 every 20 epochs), Xavier init, two-step training when CRF is included (pretrain without CRF, then fine-tune with CRF)
loss_function: Voxel-wise weighted cross-entropy (class weighting for organ imbalance); initial training with unweighted cross-entropy then fine-tuning with weighted; CRFasRNN pairwise Gibbs energy with learnable compatibility
preprocessing: Intensity normalization to zero mean and unit variance; body contour mask used to exclude background during training; data augmentation via random affine transform and random B-spline deformation (2x2x2 grid of control points)
postprocessing: None as a separate step; CRF integrated as an end-to-end trainable network module (not standalone post-processing)
datasets: ["Private dataset of 30 thoracic CT scans (patients with lung cancer or Hodgkin lymphoma)"]
dataset_size: 30 thoracic CT scans (6-fold cross-validation: 25 train / 5 test per fold)
other_metrics: {"dice_std_SM+CRF": {"esophagus": 0.04, "heart": 0.01, "trachea": 0.06, "aorta": 0.05}, "statistical_tests": "Paired t-test; SM+CRF vs FCN p<0.05 for esophagus/heart/trachea, not significant for aorta (p=0.37); CRF module gain vs base architecture mostly non-significant (p=0.30-0.79)", "baseline_notes": "OPAL label fusion beat FCN on trachea (0.80 vs 0.72); esophagus hardest organ (OPAL 0.39)"}
comparison_methods: ["FCN (baseline)", "FCN + CRF", "SharpMask (SM)", "SM + CRF (proposed)", "OPAL (Optimized PatchMatch label fusion)"]
limitations: No explicit limitations section; implicit limitations: small dataset (30 scans), trachea better segmented by OPAL than plain FCN, and CRF refinement gains largely non-significant (p=0.30-0.79); esophagus remains difficult (Dice 0.67)
future_work: Investigating new ways to incorporate context, such as auto-context models

title: Automated Segmentation of Pulmonary Lobes Using Coordination-Guided Deep Neural Networks
venue: IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI 2019)
architecture_details: V-net backbone (compression/expansion paths with skip connections) with 3D CoordConv layers (x, y, z coordinate channels normalized to [-1,1]) added in the last transition of the decoding path; PReLU instead of ReLU; group normalization instead of batch normalization; dropout 0.5; softmax output for 5 lobe classes + background; auxiliary fissure/boundary output head sharing the same network. A 2D U-Net performs lung segmentation as preprocessing.
loss_function: Dice loss for lobes + auxiliary boundary Dice loss: D_total = D_lobes + λ·D_boundary (λ=1, γ=1e-5)
preprocessing: Downsampling to 256×256×128; 2D automated lung segmentation (U-Net) to extract lung ROI and remove false responses outside the lung
postprocessing: None (fully end-to-end, no heavy post-processing)
datasets: ["LUNA16", "LKDS", "Meinian One-health Health-care Holdings", "LOLA11 (Lobe and Lung Analysis 2011)"]
dataset_size: 343 chest CT scans (71 LUNA16, 195 LKDS, 62 Meinian, 15 LOLA11); slice spacing 0.5–1.5 mm; healthy and pathological lungs
organs_segmented: ["pulmonary lobes (right upper, right middle, right lower, left upper, left lower lung lobes)"]

inference_time: ~12 s per case (overall processing time, single Tesla P100)

title: An Efficient Hybrid Model for Kidney Tumor Segmentation in CT Images
venue: IEEE 17th International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI 2020)
architecture: HybridNet: V-Net (foreground) + Submanifold Sparse Convolutional Network on point clouds (fine-grained segmentation)
architecture_details: Two-stage hybrid. Stage 1: Foreground Segmentation Network (V-Net backbone, encoder-decoder with skip connections) segments kidney+tumor foreground from background. Stage 2: Voxel-to-Point (VP) module converts foreground voxels to a sparse point cloud (z-axis stretched 6x to handle anisotropy without interpolation artifacts); Sparse Segmentation Network (SSN), a U-Net-like SSCN using submanifold sparse convolutions (hash-table storage of non-empty voxels only), classifies points as kidney vs tumor.
loss_function: Dice Loss (foreground V-Net stage); weighted Cross Entropy Loss (SSN point-cloud stage)
preprocessing: Uniform z-axis cropping to patches of size 16; intensity clipping to range [-79, 304]; intensity normalization to whole-dataset statistics; z-axis coordinates stretched 6x in VP module
postprocessing: Largest Connected Component (LCC) after V-Net foreground segmentation to remove discrete noise
datasets: ["KiTS19 (KiTS19 challenge kidney tumor CT data, ref Heller et al.)"]
dataset_size: 300 contrast-enhanced CT scans; 210 annotated (random 30 used as validation), 90 official test cases scored via online server
dice_per_organ: {"tumor": {"validation_set": 84.9, "test_set": 79.7}, "kidney": "not separately reported (V-Net foreground stage stated to reach ~0.9 Dice)"}
other_metrics: {"training_memory_usage_MiB_batch1": 2500, "latency_s_per_sample": 0.22, "params_M": 2.7, "FLOPs_per_sample": "9.3G", "note": "Claims ~9x GPU memory saving vs Roth et al. full-ROI baseline (21.6K MiB, 7.17 s/sample, 558.7G FLOPs); ablation with coordinates-only input (no intensity) achieves 60.4 valid / 60.4 test Dice"}
comparison_methods: ["V-Net (Milletari et al.)", "Roth et al. multi-scale pyramid 3D FCN (patch-based)", "Roth et al. with entire ROI as input"]

screening_notes: The paper proposes DD-UNet++ (standard U-Net++ with standard convolutions replaced by dilated convolutions in the two deepest layers, dilation rates 1/2/4/8) for segmenting bladder, rectum, and CTV on pelvic CT images of 70 post-hysterectomy patients (~13,000 slices, ~11,000 annotated). It satisfies most criteria: deep learning is the primary method (criterion 1 ✓), CT modality (criterion 4 ✓), organ segmentation including OARs (bladder, rectum) plus CTV (criterion 3 ✓), quantitative Dice evaluation (criterion 5 ✓), and a modest novel architectural modification (criterion 6 ✓). However, the network operates strictly on individual 2D slices: 'During the testing phase, all 2D CT sections in the test set were tested one by one. The input is a two-dimensional CT image, and the final output is a pixel-level classification.' There are no 3D convolutions, no adjacent-slice stacking, and no volumetric context modeling — the dilated convolutions enlarge only the in-plane (2D) receptive field. This matches exclusion criterion 3 ('Only processes 2D slices without 3D context') and fails the mandatory inclusion criterion 2 (processes 3D CT volumes, not just 2D slices independently).

loss_function: Sum of pixel-wise losses between network prediction and human-annotated label map (exact loss type not named; optimized with ADAM)

postprocessing: Vote-based labeling: 2D per-section labels projected back to original 3D locations and combined by 3D majority voting
datasets: ["Computational Anatomy CT database (Japanese research project, Tokushima University Hospital)"]
dataset_size: 240 ground-truth 3D CT scans used (228 training / 12 testing) from a database of 640 scans / 200 patients; 89 torso, 17 chest, 114 abdomen, 20 abdomen-with-pelvis
other_metrics: {"Jaccard index (IoU, 3D)": {"left kidney": 0.88, "pancreas": 0.65}, "voxel accuracy (true positive rate)": {"left kidney": 0.99, "pancreas": 0.84}}
comparison_methods: ["Authors' previous deep CNN method without localization (IU: left kidney 80%, pancreas 31%)", "Previous state-of-the-art methods (qualitative comparison only, no numbers given)"]
inference_time: Real-time 2D segmentation claimed (arbitrary CT-scan-range); no concrete timing reported
limitations: Preliminary results with only 12 test cases; evaluation limited to two organs (pancreas, left kidney); pancreas accuracy still moderate (65% IU); organ localization module not adapted/fine-tuned to the evaluation database; methods compared only against authors' own prior work with no external benchmark numbers
future_work: Apply the proposed method to improve segmentation accuracy for other anatomical structures

screening_notes: DL-CNN (Krizhevsky-style, cuda-convnet) is the primary segmentation method, generating a bladder-wall likelihood map refined by 3D level sets into inner/outer wall contours. CT modality (CT urography). Bladder wall = organ-wall segmentation, not tumor-only. Quantitative evaluation via volume intersection %. Novelty: extends prior outer-wall-only work (Cha et al. 2016) to inner+outer walls with improved outer wall results. Borderline on criterion 2: the CNN itself is 2D and applied slice-by-slice on 16x16 ROIs (no 3D convolutions); 3D context comes only from the volumetric level-set refinement and volume-based evaluation — included on the grounds that the pipeline performs volumetric segmentation rather than independent 2D slice labeling.
title: Segmentation of inner and outer bladder wall using deep-learning convolutional neural networks in CT urography
venue: SPIE Medical Imaging 2017: Computer-Aided Diagnosis (Proc. SPIE Vol. 10134)
architecture_details: 5-layer CNN: 2 convolutional layers (64 kernels each) each followed by pooling, 2 locally connected layers (64 then 32 kernels), fully connected output. Input: 16x16 pixel ROIs. Applied slice-by-slice to produce a bladder-wall likelihood map, used as an energy term in level sets to refine inner and outer wall contours.
loss_function: Not reported
preprocessing: Extraction of 240,000 16x16 pixel ROIs from training CTU scans (half centered inside bladder wall, half outside)
postprocessing: Level sets run twice (two parameter sets) on CTU scan + likelihood map to refine inner and outer bladder wall contours
datasets: ["In-house CT urography (CTU) dataset, University of Michigan (IRB-approved)"]
dataset_size: 94 CTU cases (79 training, 15 test), radiologist-outlined reference standard
other_metrics: {"volume_intersection_train_inner_wall": "90.0 ± 8.7%", "volume_intersection_train_outer_wall": "93.7 ± 3.9%", "volume_intersection_test_inner_wall": "87.6 ± 7.6%", "volume_intersection_test_outer_wall": "87.2 ± 9.3%", "note": "Dice not reported; volume intersection (VG∩VU/VG) used as overlap metric"}
comparison_methods: ["Prior DL-CNN method for outer wall only (Cha et al. 2016, Medical Physics)", "Radiologist hand-outlined reference standard"]
limitations: Contours may be over-segmented even with level sets; method may incorrectly segment parts of the prostate overlapping the outer bladder wall; inner wall under-segmentation occurs in contrast-enhanced regions.
future_work: None explicitly stated; work is part of an ongoing CAD system for bladder cancer detection in CTU (NIH grant U01CA179106).

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: 3D FCN (deep learning primary method) processing full 3D CT volumes (120x120x120), pancreas organ segmentation, contrast-enhanced portal venous CT, Dice reported, novel contribution (multi-GPU dense 3D U-Net variant, summation vs concatenation skip connection ablation, new SOTA). Study-type routing: 'method' — novel segmentation method, not an open-source framework/tooling paper.
title: Towards dense volumetric pancreas segmentation in CT using 3D fully convolutional networks
architecture_details: Custom multi-GPU 3D U-Net with same-size convolutions (zero padding) for dense whole-volume output; two variants: concatenation skip connections (25M params) vs summation skip connections (12M params, mimics residual learning); random forest bounding-box localization front-end; four resolution levels; mini-batch training with batch normalization
loss_function: Pseudo Dice score (V-Net style)
preprocessing: Random forest regression bounding box localization with margin added (100% recall guarantee); detected regions resampled to fixed 120x120x120
postprocessing: Thresholding of probability map at p(x) >= 0.5 (no other postprocessing)
datasets: ["Clinical trial gastric cancer patient abdominal CT dataset (portal venous phase, contrast-enhanced)"]
dataset_size: 147 CT scans (100 train / 47 test)
dice_per_organ: {"pancreas": "89.7 ± 3.8% (range [79.8, 94.8]) with summation skip connections; 88.3 ± 4.0% (range [76.4, 94.1]) with concatenation"}
comparison_methods: ["Original 3D U-Net cascaded/tiled (Roth et al. 2017)", "Oda et al. 2016 (RF + graph cut)", "Roth et al. 2017 (2D FCN)", "Zhou et al. 2016 (2D FCN coarse-to-fine)"]
framework: Keras with TensorFlow backend; Adam optimizer (lr 1e-2)
gpu_used: 4x NVIDIA Quadro P6000 (24 GB each) in DeepLearning BOX (uniV)
limitations: Direct comparison to other methods is difficult due to different datasets and validation schemes employed; single-organ (pancreas) focus only
future_work: Extension to multi-organ segmentation by adjusting the loss function; inclusion of anatomical constraints to guarantee topologically correct segmentation results; larger GPU memory and datasets expected to further improve performance

screening_notes: Meets most criteria superficially: 3D U-Net-like FCN (3x3x3 kernels, 64x64x64 subvolumes), 377 contrast-enhanced portal-venous abdominal CTs, multi-organ segmentation (liver, spleen, stomach, gallbladder, pancreas, artery, portal vein), quantitative Dice (89.3% +/- 6.5 test average). However, the article's stated purpose is pedagogical ('we describe how to build a 3D FCN'); the architecture is replicated from Cicek et al. 3D U-Net [21] and the loss from Milletari et al. V-Net [22] with uniform class weights; authors concede results are 'comparable' to prior work and that direct comparison is difficult due to differing datasets. The underlying novel contribution (hierarchical 3D FCN, arXiv:1704.06382, ref [44]) is published separately and should be screened instead. Confidence not higher because the demo experiment has real evaluation and could be argued as an application paper.
exclusion_reason: Tutorial/introduction article (special issue: 'Introduction to Deep Learning in Medical Image Processing') that demonstrates an existing 3D U-Net architecture with a V-Net-style Dice loss on abdominal CT; presents no new method, architecture, or significant improvement — fails include criterion 6 (novel contribution) and triggers exclusion criterion 7 (applies existing methods without methodological contribution).

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: DL-primary (improved 3D U-Net), true 3D volumetric processing (2×2×2 pooling, 32×256×256 voxels), liver organ segmentation from abdominal CT, DSC reported (0.961±0.013), and novel contribution via dilated convolution stacks, separable convolutions, extra skip concatenations, and HU-based post-processing. No exclusion criteria triggered.
title: Automatic Liver Segmentation in CT Volumes with Improved 3D U-net
architecture_details: Improved 3D U-Net: 7 dilated convolution stacks (dilation rates 1, 2, 4, 6), 8 depth-wise separable convolution layers, additional skip concatenations at intervals of two conv layers in the encoder, SeLU activation with Lecun_normal init, transposed convolution (2×2×2, stride 2) upsampling
loss_function: Not explicitly stated (validation loss monitored for model selection; Dice used as evaluation metric only)
preprocessing: 2D linear interpolation to 1mm pixel spacing; crop to 256×256 in x,y (center shifted 30px left) and 32 slices in z; HU windowing to [20,160] with values outside set to -1000; 4x data augmentation via random small-range rotation and translation
postprocessing: Binarize probability map at 0.5; restore to 512×512 via background fill and pixel-spacing interpolation; mask optimization using liver HU>0 (multiply mask with original image, re-binarize) to remove false positives
datasets: ["Private abdominal CT dataset (one hospital, Sichuan Cancer Hospital & Institute)"]
dataset_size: 960 abdominal CT slices (source scans have 89–314 slices each); 70/20/10 train/val/test split; patient count not stated
comparison_methods: ["Lu et al. 2018 (multi-dimensional graph cut + shape info, DSC 0.94)", "Yang et al. 2017 (adversarial image-to-image network, DSC 0.95)"]
training_time: ~4 min per epoch, 50 epochs (~3.3 hours total)
limitations: Fixed HU range [20,160] and fixed 256×256 crop size fail on some special data, potentially causing false negatives in segmentation results
future_work: Not explicitly stated

screening_notes: DL is primary method (CNN encoder-decoder, ResNet encoder, ASPP); segments liver (organ) on CT; quantitative metrics reported (Dice 0.9485, mIoU 0.9508); novel contribution (3D anisotropic multi-axis ensemble + step transfer learning). Borderline on 3D criterion: no true 3D convolutions — it is a 2.5D approach (three 2D networks on axial/coronal/sagittal slices, predictions fused). However, it exploits 3D contextual information from the volume, so the exclusion 'only 2D slices without 3D context' does not apply. Not a framework paper.
title: 3D Anisotropic Convolutional Neural Network with Step Transfer Learning for Liver Segmentation
architecture: Encoder-decoder CNN with ResNet encoder, atrous convolutions and ASPP; 3D anisotropic ensemble of three 2D segmentation networks (axial, coronal, sagittal)
architecture_details: ResNet-50/101/152 encoders (ResNet-152 best); residual blocks, atrous (dilated) layers, Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling, skip connections, bilinear upsampling decoder; inspired by DeepLabV3; each network takes 3 consecutive slices as input (2.5D); predictions from the three orthogonal axes are averaged at inference; Step Transfer Learning (freeze pre-trained encoder, train stochastic layers first, then fine-tune all)
loss_function: Lovász-Softmax loss
preprocessing: Slice cropping along axial, coronal and sagittal axes; resolution 512x512 (sagittal), 512x64 (axial/coronal); online data augmentation (random rotation, zoom, shear, horizontal flip); Batch Normalization before residual blocks
postprocessing: Averaging/fusion of segmentation predictions from the three orthogonal axes
datasets: ["LiTS (Liver Tumor Segmentation Challenge; written 'LiST' in paper)"]
dataset_size: 131 training + 30 testing 3D CT scans
comparison_methods: ["Isotropic single-axis baselines (axial/coronal/sagittal)", "Traditional transfer learning (TTL) vs Step Transfer Learning (STL)", "ResNet-50 vs ResNet-101 vs ResNet-152 encoder variants"]
training_time: ~3 days per single model, 20 epochs, batch size 4, Adam (lr=0.0001)
limitations: Not explicitly enumerated; authors note the model needs performance improvement to achieve more precise segmentation; approach is liver-only and 2.5D rather than fully 3D
future_work: Improve segmentation precision; apply the framework to other segmentation tasks (heart, brain tumor) and other modalities (X-ray, MRI)

screening_notes: Borderline on two criteria, resolved toward include. (1) DL-primary: final segmentation comes from DRLSE level set, but U-Net provides the automatic initial contour and drives the gain (0.82 Dice vs 0.37-0.66 for pure level-set baselines); contribution is the CNN-based hybrid, so DL counts as primary. (2) 3D: abstract claims 3D whole-pancreas segmentation, but the described U-Net is 2D (3x3 convs, 2x2 max pooling) and Dice is evaluated on 20 randomly selected 2D slices; no explicit 3D convolutions. Flag for reviewer attention on criterion 2/3. Passes organ (pancreas), CT modality, quantitative metrics (Dice + VD), and novelty (novel CNN+DRLSE combination with fractional differential preprocessing). Not a framework paper.
title: Convolutional Neural Networks Based Level Set Framework for Pancreas Segmentation from CT Images
architecture: Hybrid U-Net + Distance Regularized Level Set Evolution (DRLSE)
architecture_details: 2D U-Net (23 conv layers, 3x3 convs + ReLU + 2x2 max pooling, 1x1 final conv) generates initial pancreas region; signed-distance initial contour phi0 derived from U-net output; DRLSE energy (distance regularization + length + area terms, mu=0.2, eps=1.5, alpha=5, beta=-3) evolves final boundary
loss_function: DRLSE energy functional (regularization term + weighted length/area terms); U-Net training loss not specified
preprocessing: Fractional differential enhancement to improve pancreas-to-surrounding-tissue contrast
postprocessing: Level set evolution (DRLSE) refining the U-Net initial contour
dataset_size: 20 CT scans
comparison_methods: ["CV model", "GAC model", "LBF", "IVC"]
limitations: Very small dataset (20 CT scans); U-Net trained on few samples extracts only part of pancreas; evaluation performed on 2D slices
future_work: Further studies with more data to check possible algorithm improvements

screening_notes: Passes all inclusion criteria: 3D U-Net backbone (DL component), 3D pancreatic CT volumes (organ segmentation, not tumor), quantitative metrics (Dice 0.78, MSE 4.2, accuracy/precision/recall/F1), novel contribution (shadowed-sets uncertain-region determination + interactive correction framework). Minor caveat: the primary novelty is the shadowed-sets interactive correction rather than the network itself, but the pipeline is explicitly DL-based and DL (3D U-Net) is the segmentation engine, so exclusion criterion 2 does not apply. Confidence capped at 0.85 due to the interactive/DL hybrid nature and small private dataset.
title: Deep Interactive Segmentation of Uncertain Regions with Shadowed Sets
venue: ISICDM 2019 (ACM International Symposium on Image and Data Fusion)
architecture_details: 3D U-Net (Çiçek et al.) for initial segmentation, followed by a shadowed-sets-based interactive correction loop: expert scribbles/points define local ROI (9×9×2 voxels), k most similar reference labels (k=8) selected via similarity cost, averaged into a probability map, thresholded by shadowed-sets α*=0.375 into confident foreground/background/uncertain regions, with second-round expert correction using Gaussian-modeled interactions
loss_function: Not specified (training loss for 3D U-Net not stated in paper)
preprocessing: Images resized to 256×256; data augmentation (translation and scale transforms)
postprocessing: Shadowed-sets thresholding of probability map into confident/uncertain regions; two rounds of expert interaction (points/scribbles) with Gaussian distribution-based label correction
datasets: ["Changhai Hospital pancreatic CT dataset (private, 20 patients with pancreatic endocrine neoplasms)"]
dataset_size: 20 CT volumes; 512×512×(36–74) voxels, 0.66×0.66×1.5 mm³; 4-fold cross validation
other_metrics: {"MSE": 4.2, "MSE_3d_unet_baseline": 6.3, "accuracy_precision_recall_f1": "reported in Figure 5(b) as plots only, exact values not extractable", "case_example_dice": "82% (proposed) vs 66% (3D U-Net) on showcased case"}
comparison_methods: ["Otsu threshold segmentation", "3D U-Net", "ablation: first interaction only vs final (second interaction)"]
limitations: Not explicitly stated. Implicit limitations: very small single-center private dataset (20 scans, pancreatic endocrine neoplasms only), requires clinician interaction (semi-automatic, not fully automatic), single organ (pancreas), Dice (78%) below state-of-the-art automatic methods on public benchmarks at the time
future_work: Not explicitly stated; conclusion suggests clinical use of uncertainty maps to help clinicians analyze uncertain organ boundaries for diagnosis/treatment

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) deep learning (fully convolutional networks) is the primary method; (2) 3 of 4 benchmarked models operate on 3D CT volumes (2D U-Net included only as baseline); (3) segments lungs/thoracic cavity (organs) — note only lungs, not multi-organ; (4) CT modality; (5) quantitative metrics (Dice, HD95, ASSD) with statistical tests; (6) contribution is a controlled head-to-head architecture benchmark on the 402-scan PleThora dataset with identical pre/post-processing and clinical-variable stratification, which qualifies under the 'benchmark' study-type routing rather than as a novel architecture. Not excluded under E7 because the disentangled pipeline comparison and stratified error analysis constitute a substantive benchmarking contribution, consistent with the v2 routing that permits 'benchmark' papers.
title: Segmenting Thoracic Cavities with Neoplastic Lesions: A Head-to-head Benchmark with Fully Convolutional Neural Networks
venue: ACM-BCB '21 (11th ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology, and Health Informatics)
architecture: Benchmark of four fully convolutional architectures: 3D U-Net, V-Net (modified), 2D U-Net, two-stage 3D U-Net (best performer)
architecture_details: 3D U-Net per Cec et al. (3x3x3 convs, 2x2x2 max-pooling stride 2, BN+ReLU, 1x1x1 output conv); V-Net modified: kernel size 5->3 stride 1, dropout added except first/last residual blocks, final 16x compression block removed; 2D U-Net = 3D U-Net with all operations replaced by 2D counterparts; two-stage 3D U-Net adapted from AAPM 2017 UVA challenge codebase for two-class (left/right lung) coarse-then-organ-specific segmentation
loss_function: Differentiable (soft) Dice coefficient loss with Adam optimizer
preprocessing: Resample to modal spacing; mask-based cropping of compact lung region; pad to 460x364x130; resample to (2.5, 2.5, 4.0) mm; pad to 104x208x208 voxels; intensity clipping to [-250, 0]; two-stage model additionally crops 72x192x120 sub-volumes around coarse lung predictions
postprocessing: Contour cleaning: extract closed object contours, keep largest connected component per lung; predictions rescaled to original resolution via nearest-neighbor interpolation
datasets: ["PleThora (pleural effusion and thoracic cavity segmentations in diseased lungs, The Cancer Imaging Archive)"]
dataset_size: 402 CT scans from cancer patients (train:val:test = 7:1:2)
other_metrics: {"HD95_mm_after_postprocessing": {"3d_unet": {"left": 4.964, "right": 5.49}, "vnet": {"left": 5.712, "right": 5.308}, "2d_unet": {"left": 6.005, "right": 6.254}, "two_stage": {"left": 5.013, "right": 5.088}, "reviewers": {"left": 2.623, "right": 1.148}, "note": "Text states 3D U-Net best on right-lung HD95, though table values favor two-stage model; minor internal inconsistency"}, "ASSD_mm_after_postprocessing": {"3d_unet": {"left": 1.485, "right": 1.495}, "vnet": {"left": 1.591, "right": 1.525}, "2d_unet": {"left": 1.71, "right": 1.789}, "two_stage": {"left": 1.661, "right": 1.601}, "reviewers": {"left": 0.676, "right": 0.191}}, "statistical_analysis": "Mann-Whitney U / two-sided tests vs 2D U-Net baseline; two-stage 3D U-Net significantly better (p<0.05) for right-lung DC and HD95; contour cleaning improvements not significant", "clinical_stratification": "3D U-Net performance stratified by age, gender, stage, histology; worse for stage I disease, female patients (potential sex bias), and collapsed lungs"}
comparison_methods: ["2D U-Net (baseline)", "V-Net (modified)", "3D U-Net", "Two-stage 3D U-Net (AAPM 2017 UVA model)", "Human expert inter-observer agreement (reference)"]
framework: Not explicitly stated (V-Net from public GitHub repo; two-stage model adapted from AAPM 2017 challenge codebase)
training_time: 50 epochs; per-epoch: 3D U-Net 25.04 min, V-Net 8.03 min, 2D U-Net 12.73 min, two-stage stage-1 7.31 min + stage-2 12.52 min; parameters: 3D U-Net 19.07M, V-Net 9.32M, 2D U-Net 6.82M, two-stage 3.15M + 12.60M
limitations: Poor performance on rare anatomic outliers (e.g., severely collapsed lung); PleThora, though largest of its kind, still insufficiently large/diverse to represent outliers; left lung segmented slightly worse than right; performance gap to inter-observer agreement remains; two-stage approach requires training up to three models and is not time-efficient in training or inference; 3D models demand high GPU memory; patch-based methods not evaluated; potential sex bias observed
future_work: Expand training data for challenging anatomic cases; evaluate imaging jointly with holistic patient characteristics from multiple data sources; focus future effort on difficult samples; apply segmentations to downstream tasks (treatment planning, prognosis, survival prediction)

screening_notes: Passes criteria 1-4 (3D U-Net as segmentation method, volumetric 256×256×192 processing, liver segmentation, nonenhanced CT). Fails on evaluation and novelty: segmentation performance is only reported indirectly as a 0.06% failure rate (7/11,676 scans); the paper's contribution is epidemiological (steatosis prevalence in n=9,552 cohort, longitudinal analysis), not a segmentation method or its evaluation. Primary purpose is liver fat quantification, using segmentation as a means.
exclusion_reason: Exclusion criterion 7: applies an existing segmentation method without methodological contribution — the modified 3D U-Net with CycleGAN domain-transfer augmentation was developed in a separate technical publication (Sandfort et al., ref 24, 'submitted'); this paper only applies it. Also fails inclusion criterion 6: no segmentation metrics (Dice, IoU, Hausdorff) reported — all quantitative evaluation (r²=0.93, ±2.7 HU agreement, steatosis-category sensitivity/specificity) measures downstream fat quantification, not segmentation accuracy.

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: 3D U-Net as primary method (DL focus), processes 3D CT volumes with patch-based 3D context, segments the spleen (organ, not lesion) on contrast-enhanced thorax-abdomen CT, reports Dice/Hausdorff/ASSD/volume metrics. Novel contribution: two-stage training with data-driven relevant-case selection (system A on 100 scans -> selects 300 informative cases -> system B on 400 scans), improving Dice 0.950 -> 0.962, plus observer study showing clinical utility for splenic volume change assessment. Not a framework/tooling paper -> study_type 'method'.
title: Fully Automatic Volume Measurement of the Spleen at CT Using Deep Learning
architecture_details: Patch-based 3D U-Net with mirroring for border handling; two-stage training: system A trained from scratch on 100 annotated scans, then system A used to select 300 relevant scans from 1000, which were manually corrected and added to train system B (400 training scans total)
loss_function: Not reported (model selection per epoch by Dice score; early stopping after 10 epochs without improvement)
preprocessing: HU clipping to reported range 2500-1400 HU (likely -2500 to 1400); resampling to 1x1x1 mm (cubic interpolation for scans, nearest neighbor for masks); patch extraction due to 3D U-Net memory footprint
postprocessing: Patch-wise prediction stitched together, thresholded at 0.5, largest connected component retained, resampled back to original resolution (nearest neighbor)
datasets: ["In-house Radboud University Medical Center thorax-abdomen CT dataset (oncology patients, contrast-enhanced)"]
dataset_size: 1100 scans from 1100 patients used: 100 training (dataset A) + 1000 for relevant-case selection (dataset B, 300 selected) + 50 test (dataset C) + 500-patient observer-experiment set (dataset D, enriched subset D100 = 100 patients / 200 scans)
comparison_methods: ["Splenic index equation", "System A (3D U-Net, 100 training scans)", "Independent human observer (Dice 0.964, P = .834 vs system B)", "Prior spleen segmentation work (Gauriau, Wood, Gloger, Zhou, Wolz, Tong, Huo, Roth, Landman, Okada, Gibson, Linguraru)"]
limitations: Irregular segmentations in patients with severe body distortions; possible false positives after splenectomy; no quantitative validation on the large dataset (annotation effort); relevant-case selection done by a single observer (potential bias); independent observer was a trained medical student, not an experienced radiologist; single-center data
future_work: Define better SVC thresholds for clinical practice; quantitative validation on larger annotated sets; multicenter training and validation; prospective clinical validation and radiologist workflow-impact studies

screening_notes: Passes all criteria: deep learning is the primary method (five 3D U-Net models), operates on 3D contrast-enhanced CT volumes, segments liver anatomy (whole liver, 8 Couinaud segments, hepatic/portal veins), and reports quantitative evaluation (Spearman r=0.99 vs manual volumetry, AUC=0.89, sensitivity/specificity, Bland-Altman). Borderline points: (1) no voxel-overlap metrics (Dice/IoU/HD) reported — evaluation is volumetric agreement and clinical candidate categorization, accepted under 'etc.' in criterion 5; (2) novelty is at the system level (DL-FLRVS pipeline + external clinical validation), not architecture — authors explicitly use the standard 3D U-Net (Çiçek et al.) and acknowledge in limitations that this precludes comparison with nnU-Net/transformers. Counted as a novel clinical method/system rather than 'existing methods only'. Not a framework paper: no open-source code, license, or versioned release (data 'available on reasonable request' only).
title: Deep learning-based volumetry of the future liver remnants and prediction of candidates for major hepatectomy
architecture: 3D U-Net (ensemble of five 3D U-Net models, DL-FLRVS)
architecture_details: Five separate 3D U-Net models (per Çiçek et al. 2016) for hepatic lesion detection, whole liver, 8 Couinaud liver segments, hepatic veins, and portal veins; combined pipeline with FLR calculation formulas and rule-based candidate categorization (healthy/fatty/cirrhotic thresholds 20%/30%/40%)
preprocessing: Not detailed in main text (in Appendix E1); cohort inclusion restricted to contrast-enhanced CT with slice thickness ≤ 2 mm
datasets: ["Internal training cohorts (Hospital-1, Peking University First Hospital)", "External validation cohort-1 (Hospital-2, diverse liver conditions)", "External validation cohort-2 (Hospital-2, post-hepatectomy candidates)"]
dataset_size: Training: 307/170/170/170/492 CT scans per model (Hospital-1, 2283 screened); validation: 146 + 32 patients (Hospital-2, 1774 screened)
other_metrics: {"Spearman_r_FLR_vs_manual": 0.99, "AUC_candidate_categorization_DL-FLRVS": 0.89, "AUC_hepatic_VCAR": 0.86, "sensitivity_DL-FLRVS": 0.86, "specificity_DL-FLRVS": 0.75, "best_cutoff_FLR%_DL-FLRVS": "29.21%", "note": "No Dice/IoU/Hausdorff reported; evaluation is volumetric agreement and clinical categorization"}
comparison_methods: ["hepatic VCAR (semi-automated GE workstation volumetry)", "manual volumetry by human doctors", "prior DL FLR studies (Le et al., Ruskó et al., Butdee et al., Chen et al.)"]
limitations: Manual volumetry used as reference standard instead of actual post-resection remnant (suboptimal external validation); no functional volumetry (Gd-EOB-DTPA MRI); well-established 3D U-Net used, precluding comparison with contemporary architectures (nnU-Net, transformer-based); retrospective two-hospital study; Child-Pugh B/C excluded
future_work: Prospective validation against actual post-resection liver remnants; benchmarking against nnU-Net and transformer-based segmentation models; MRI-based functional volumetry integration

screening_notes: Passes all inclusion criteria: (1) DL primary method — novel 2D–3D hybrid CNN; (2) true volumetric processing — 3D V-Net branch on 64-slice volumes with 2D–3D feature fusion, not slice-independent; (3) segments lung lobes (anatomical organ substructures, not tumors/lesions); (4) CT only (5 mm radiotherapy planning CT); (5) quantitative metrics (DSC, HD95, MSD, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy); (6) novel architecture contribution. Not a framework paper — no toolkit/release. Note for reviewers: lung LOBES are organ subunits rather than whole organs; include if review scope covers lung/organ substructure segmentation.
title: A 2D–3D hybrid convolutional neural network for lung lobe auto-segmentation on standard slice thickness computed tomography of patients receiving radiotherapy
architecture: 2D–3D hybrid CNN (3D V-Net branch + dense-connected 2D CNN with hybrid feature fusion module)
architecture_details: 3D branch: V-Net encoder–decoder (PReLU, 2×2×2 stride-2 downsampling) extracting 3D context. 2D branch: V-Net-like encoder with three dense blocks for intra-slice edge/texture info. Fusion: 2D features upsampled, 64 slices stacked to 256×256×64×32, concatenated with 3D features, refined by 3×3×3 conv, 2-channel output + softmax.
loss_function: Dice loss
preprocessing: Normalization; resampling to 1×1×3 mm; crop to 256×256; volumes of 64 consecutive slices (stride 1), rescaled to 512×512×64 for 3D branch; 2D slices normalized to 0–1, only slices containing at least one lung lobe kept; data augmentation (random translation, scaling, rotation)
postprocessing: None performed (authors explicitly note no post-processing optimization)
datasets: ["Institutional retrospective dataset (Shanghai Chest Hospital) — locally advanced stage IIIA(N2) NSCLC radiotherapy planning CT"]
dataset_size: 105 patients (50 train / 20 val / 35 test); 7090 CT slices (4705 train+val, 2385 test); 350 lobe contours pre-augmentation
organs_segmented: ["left upper lobe", "left lower lobe", "right upper lobe", "right middle lobe", "right lower lobe"]
comparison_methods: ["PDV-Net (Imran et al.) — literature comparison on thin-slice LIDC data", "3D U-Net (Park et al.) — literature comparison on COPD data", "Harrison et al. HNN", "George et al. HNN + random walker"]
training_time: Not reported (trained 1000 epochs, batch size 1, Adam lr=0.001, weight decay 1e-8)
limitations: Stated: no post-processing optimization was performed, which may affect some segmentation results. Implicit in text: single-center retrospective data, single expert observer ground truth, small cohort (105 patients), and RML remains hardest (DSC 0.9003) due to small volume and fissure visibility at 5 mm slice thickness.
future_work: Further optimize the model to achieve more precise lung lobe segmentation; extend to lobar-level treatment planning, dose evaluation, and outcome prediction.

screening_notes: Borderline case. Meets: DL as primary method (DpnUNet), planning CT modality, quantitative metrics (DSC, 95HD, sensitivity, specificity), multi-structure segmentation. Fails Novel Contribution: no new architecture or training method is proposed; the claimed novelty (first fine-tuning study for rectal cancer DLAS, generalizability across CT simulators) is clinical/deployment-level, and the performance gains come from routine fine-tuning of an existing vendor model. Also targets CTV (non-organ) in addition to only 3 OARs (bladder, femoral heads, small intestine), and 3D convolutions are never explicitly stated (likely volumetric but unconfirmed). Would flip to INCLUDE only if the review scope counts commercial-model adaptation studies as methodological contributions.
exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution (Exclusion #7): the segmentation backbone (DpnUNet) is adopted from prior work (Wu et al.) and commercialized as RT-Mind-AI; the study's contribution is standard localized fine-tuning (Adam, class-weighted cross-entropy, 5-fold CV) plus clinical validation of a commercial product, not a new method, architecture, or methodological advance.

screening_notes: All 6 inclusion criteria met: (1) modified Mask R-CNN is the primary segmentation method; (2) 2.5D input with adjacent slices plus tri-planar (axial/sagittal/coronal) consensus procedure building a 3D mask — provides 3D context, so not excluded under '2D slices only', though is_3d=false since no true 3D convolutions; (3) segments liver and kidneys; (4) CT (contrast-enhanced + low-dose), SPECT used only for downstream dosimetry; (5) Dice reported (liver 93.4%, kidney 94.1–94.6%) with 5-fold validation; (6) novel contribution: empirically optimized Mask R-CNN (2.5D input, 28x28 RoI pooling, 256x256 masks, P1/C1 dropped, consensus mode) with 20% memory reduction and ablation vs. unmodified baseline (15% lower accuracy). Study-type: method (not an open-source framework/tooling paper — no code release). Confidence docked to 0.85 solely due to the 2.5D vs 3D judgment call.
title: Automated and robust organ segmentation for 3D-based internal dose calculation
architecture_details: 2.5D Mask R-CNN with ResNet50-FPN backbone: adjacent axial slices as multi-channel input; RoI-pooling enlarged 7x7 to 28x28; binary mask output 256x256; P1/C1 layers excluded from RPN; optional consensus mode training/predicting in 3 orthogonal planes with voxel-wise majority voting. Two-stage: RPN RoI proposal then mask/classification heads
loss_function: Multi-task loss L = Lcls + Lbox + Lmask (5 joint losses: 2 classification, 2 bounding-box regression, 1 binary cross-entropy mask loss)
preprocessing: Only CT windowing with HU threshold [-100, 200]; no spatial normalization (explicitly eliminated)
postprocessing: Linear interpolation of masks across failed slices (~2% slice failure rate); linear interpolation of masks 256x256 to 512x512 at inference; 3 mm mask expansion (Gaussian PSF, sigma 3 mm) before application to SPECT for activity retrieval
datasets: ["LiTS challenge (dataset 1)", "KiTS19 challenge (dataset 2)", "Internal multi-centre CT (dataset 3, 6 hospitals)", "Internal SPECT/CT dosimetry (dataset 4, 8 patients)", "ImageNet (backbone pretraining/transfer learning)"]
dataset_size: LiTS: 170 abdominal CTs (70/10/20 train/val/test); KiTS19: 200 CTs (60/20/20); dataset 3: 12 contrast-enhanced + 48 low-dose CTs; dataset 4: 8 patients, 4 SPECT/CT time points each
comparison_methods: ["Yuan 2017 (hierarchical conv-deconv, LiTS)", "Bi et al. 2017 (cascaded deep residual, LiTS)", "Delmoral et al. 2019 (dilated FCN, LiTS)", "Chlebus et al. 2018 (FCN, LiTS)", "Okada et al. 2007 (atlas/SSM, non-DL)", "Santini et al. 2019 (multi-stage DL, KiTS19)", "Lin et al. 2006 (computer-aided kidney seg, non-DL)"]
training_time: ~20 min per epoch (batch size 2) on 2x Titan XP; liver: 50 epochs heads-frozen + 150 full; kidney: 50 + 100 epochs + 50 fine-tuning; 5-fold repeated
inference_time: 2.5 s per 2.5D slice on 1.7 GHz Intel Core i7 CPU; <3 s for entire liver or both kidneys on GTX 1070
limitations: Small dosimetry cohort (8 patients in dataset 4); automated segmentation does not remove need for expert supervision/correction, mainly due to SPECT-LDCT co-registration misalignment; strict fixed 3 mm spill-out margin caused 25% dose deviation in one patient (resolved with 6 mm margin); no true 3D spatial context as in fully 3D CNNs; lacks per-patient tuning of spill-out

screening_notes: nnU-Net V2 segments 23 whole-body structures on the CT component of SPECT/CT, so it superficially touches the review topic, but segmentation performance is never evaluated and the novelty claims (CCS dose kernel, automated multi/single-time-point dosimetry, SaaS deployment) all belong to radiopharmaceutical dosimetry. Also, evaluation is on 10 patients with dose-rate comparisons — no segmentation ground-truth comparison. Correct venue to route this is a dosimetry/theranostics review, not a 3D organ segmentation review. Not a framework paper per v2 routing (SimpleDose is a closed dosimetry SaaS, not an open-source segmentation toolkit; no license or versioned release reported).
exclusion_reason: Dosimetry pipeline paper (SimpleDose), not a CT organ segmentation paper. Fails multiple S3 criteria: (1) deep learning is not the primary method — the paper's contribution is a collapsed-cone-superposition dosimetry workflow; segmentation is a supporting step using off-the-shelf nnU-Net V2 trained on public datasets (TotalSegmentator, HaN-Seg), with no segmentation methodological contribution beyond an HU-threshold rule for bone marrow (exclusion criteria 2 and 7); (2) primary modality is whole-body SPECT/CT nuclear medicine dosimetry, not CT-based segmentation (exclusion criterion 4); (3) no segmentation metrics reported — no Dice, IoU, or Hausdorff anywhere; all quantitative results are dose-rate percentage deviations vs MIRDcalc/LDM (exclusion criterion 6 for segmentation evaluation, inclusion criterion 5 unmet).

screening_notes: Included with moderate confidence. (1) Deep learning (2D U-Net) is the primary method. (2) Although no 3D convolutions are used, the pipeline processes full 3D CT volumes via tri-planar consensus (transversal/sagittal/coronal stacks with voxel-wise probability averaging), which the paper explicitly states 'implicitly incorporates 3D information' — this satisfies the volumetric criterion and is not the excluded '2D slices without 3D context' case (borderline: is_3d=false at convolution level). (3) Segments anatomical structures including organs (lungs, trachea, cardiac blood pool/chambers, eyes) plus bone structures; 5 of 6 tasks are CT (one fetal MRI task), so CT criterion is met. (4) Reports Dice, Jaccard, 95th-percentile and median surface distances. (5) Methodological contribution: pre-configured generalizable framework with data-efficiency analysis (3–40 subject training ablation, zero-shot knee inference), though novelty is moderate (consensus 2D U-Net approach builds on prior work and no external baseline comparisons, e.g., nnU-Net, are performed). Routed to 'method' rather than 'framework' study type: although titled a 'framework', it is implemented in Matlab R2022a and embedded in commercial software (Segment 3DPrint, Medviso AB) with no open-source code release, failing F1 (open-source requirement).
title: Generalizable deep learning framework for 3D medical image segmentation using limited training data
architecture_details: Mathworks Matlab R2022a implementation of standard 2D U-Net (3x3 convolutions, 'same' padding, encoder depth 4); each 3D volume is resampled to isotropic resolution and split into transversal, sagittal, and coronal 2D stacks; the same single 2D U-Net is applied to 128x128 patches of each stack; final voxel-wise classification by averaging probabilities across the three orientations (implicit 3D context, no 3D convolutions); patch-based instead of full-volume segmentation for memory efficiency
loss_function: Cross-entropy loss (Adam optimizer, lr 0.001, L2 regularization 1e-4, gradient threshold L2 norm)
preprocessing: Resampling to isotropic resolution (highest of in-plane or through-plane of original DICOM); volume split into three orthogonal 2D stacks; subdivision into 128x128 patches with overlap; extensive augmentation (global 3D rotation, 2D rotation, scaling, mirroring, transpose, white/streak noise, brightness/contrast in HU, Gaussian blur, sharpening)
postprocessing: Object filling; removal of objects < 0.1 ml; class-specific probability thresholding (50%/25%/12.5%); selection of n-largest connected objects (26-connectivity); anatomical touch constraint (trachea required to touch lung parenchyma)
datasets: ["Skåne University Hospital 3D Centre cohorts (skeletal, oculo-cranial, mandibulo-cranial, congenital heart, pulmonary-tracheal)", "The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) - 8 skeletal cases", "Fetal MRI cohort (Ryd et al. 2022)"]

screening_notes: Meets all 6 inclusion criteria: (1) primary method is a CNN (2.5D U-Net with novel hybrid attention); (2) 2.5D architecture captures 3D context — first two encoder layers are 3D convolutions, input is 3 adjacent slices, multi-view predictions fused into 3D volume via majority voting — so it is NOT excluded under the '2D slices without 3D context' rule, though note it is not a fully-3D network; (3) segments pancreas (organ); (4) CT only (NIH pancreas dataset, 82 abdominal CT scans); (5) quantitative DSC with mean/max/min/std plus ablation study; (6) novel contribution: new 2.5D architecture combining 2D/3D convs, new hybrid spatial+channel attention module, achieving 86.61±3.47 DSC vs prior SOTA. Minor caveat lowering confidence: borderline 2.5D vs 3D classification.
title: Multi-scale U-like network with attention mechanism for automatic pancreas segmentation
architecture: 2.5D U-Net with hybrid attention (multi-scale U-like network)
architecture_details: U-shaped encoder/decoder (4 blocks each) where the first two encoder layers are 3D convolutions and remaining layers are 2D convolutions; dense convolution blocks (6 conv layers) with skip connections in encoder/decoder; proposed hybrid attention module (spatial attention + channel attention with avg/max pooling) integrated into skip connections; cascaded coarse-to-fine framework following Zhou et al. with three view-specific models (sagittal, axial, coronal) per stage and majority-vote fusion into a 3D binary volume
loss_function: Dice loss (DSC reformulated as loss)
preprocessing: HU clipping to [-100, 240], rescaling to [0, 255], slice resizing to 224x224, stacking of 3 adjacent slices as 3-channel input; slices with >100 pancreas pixels used for coarse-stage training
postprocessing: Multi-view prediction fusion via majority voting into 3D volume; coarse segmentation mask (with added frame margin) used to crop a smaller volume for the fine stage
dataset_size: 82 contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans (512x512xL, L in [181,466]), 4-fold cross-validation

limitations: No dedicated limitations section; authors note in Fig 7 discussion that the pancreas boundary is not predicted very well; single small dataset (82 scans, 4-fold CV), single organ, 2.5D rather than fully volumetric modeling

title: Liver tumor segmentation method combining multi-axis attention and conditional generative adversarial networks
architecture: MA-cGAN: U-Net-based 3D generator with multi-axis attention + 3-layer convolutional conditional GAN discriminator

screening_notes: Open-source, containerized platform (MHub.ai) standardizing inference-time distribution of 30 peer-reviewed medical imaging AI models, 22 of which are segmentation models (18 for CT). screening_notes: DL (modified 3D U-Net) is used and is volumetric on CT, and liver/spleen are segmented — but segmentation is instrumental infrastructure from prior work, not the paper's contribution. The novel element is clinical: HU threshold tables for PDFF-based steatosis categories. Fails INCLUDE criteria 5 (no segmentation metrics) and 6 (no segmentation methodological novelty). A clinical validation/application paper, out of scope for a review on 3D organ segmentation methods.
exclusion_reason: Exclusion criterion 7: applies existing DL segmentation methods without methodological contribution. The modified 3D U-Net hepatosplenic segmentation tool was previously published (refs 15, 19, 20 in the paper: 'The methodology for automated hepatosplenic assessment has been previously described in detail'); this paper only applies that existing tool to a new clinical task (steatosis categorization on contrast-enhanced CT). Secondary support: no segmentation quality metrics (Dice, IoU, Hausdorff) are reported — all quantitative results (ROC-AUC, sensitivity/specificity) evaluate HU attenuation thresholds for steatosis classification, not segmentation performance.

screening_notes: DL is primary method (three 2D U-Nets); CT modality; segments kidney (organ) + tumor, so not tumor-only; quantitative metrics reported (per-class precision/recall/F1). Borderline on criterion 2: segmentation uses 2D convolutions on axial slices, but the pipeline adds explicit 3D context via volumetric validation (volume thresholds, center-of-mass depth position, bounding-cube intersection, cross-frame consistency), so it does not meet the '2D without 3D context' exclusion. is_3d=false for convolutions. Novel contribution is modest (logical ensemble + rule-based 3D validation) but sufficient to pass the 'existing methods only' exclusion. title: Kidney and Kidney Tumor Segmentation using a Logical Ensemble of U-nets with Volumetric Validation
architecture_details: Three standard 2D U-Nets: (1) lax kidney+tumor, (2) strict kidney+tumor, (3) tumor-only; outputs fused via logical bitwise AND then summed to labels (background=0, kidney=1, tumor=2). Encoder: 9 conv layers, 4 pooling, 2 dropout (50%); decoder: 13 conv layers, 4 up-sampling; 4 skip connections; ReLU activations, sigmoid output
loss_function: Weighted binary cross-entropy (Adam optimizer, lr=1e-4, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99)
preprocessing: Resize 512x512, normalize to 0-255 uint8, histogram equalization, Otsu thresholding, median (9x9) and mean (15x15) filtering, flood-fill, morphological opening (99x99 kernel) to remove patient table, centering/zooming to body bounding box (smoothing via 4th-order polynomial), downsize to 256x256
postprocessing: Volumetric validation on stacked 2D predictions: kidneys kept if volume >19,000 normalized units, center of mass within central 60% of scan depth, present on >1 frame; tumors kept if volume >350, center of mass within 80% depth, major axis >10, minor axis >3, present on >1 frame, sphericity >0.29; tumor relabeled by intersection with kidney bounding cube
dataset_size: 210 kidney cancer patients (45,424 frames; 16,356 with kidney, 5,696 with tumor); 80:10:10 train/val/test split per model
dice_per_organ: {"kidney": 0.8497, "kidney_tumor": 0.5019, "note": "Per-class pixel-wise F1 after volumetric validation (Dice-equivalent); Dice not explicitly reported; mean kidney+tumor F1 = 0.6758"}
gpu_used: NVIDIA Tesla K80 (12 GB, via Google Colaboratory)
limitations: Performance below the level required for clinical application; poor tumor precision (0.40) due to over-segmentation of tumor regions; 2D models lack depth information; preprocessing failed to fully remove artifacts (patient table, clothing/blanket in case 88); no clear relationship between organ volume and performance to guide improvements; no comparison against other methods yet

screening_notes: Meets all 6 inclusion criteria: (1) DL primary — 3D residual attention U-Net; (2) 3D — RA-UNet-II processes 224×224×32 volumetric patches (only coarse localization stage RA-UNet-I is 2D); (3) segments liver (organ) plus tumors, so 'only tumors' exclusion does not apply; (4) CT only (LiTS, 3DIRCADb); (5) reports Dice, Jaccard, VOE, RVD, ASSD, MSD; (6) novel — first application of attention residual mechanism in 3D medical segmentation. Study type: method. Not a framework paper — it's a novel architecture, so F1-F3 and framework template fields not applicable.
title: RA-UNet: A Hybrid Deep Attention-Aware Network to Extract Liver and Tumor in CT Scans
architecture: RA-UNet (residual attention-aware U-Net), two-stage cascade: RA-UNet-I (2D, coarse liver localization) + RA-UNet-II (3D, liver and tumor segmentation)
architecture_details: 3D U-Net base with stacked residual blocks (BN-ReLU-Conv) and attention residual learning modules (trunk branch + soft mask branch with encoder-decoder, depths D=0..3); ~4M parameters; trained from scratch; sigmoid output; patch size 224×224×32 (liver) and 128×128×32 (tumor)
loss_function: Dice loss (V-Net style, Milletari et al. 2016)
preprocessing: HU windowing [-100, 200] to remove irrelevant tissues; zero-mean and min-max normalization; downsampling to 256×256 for localization stage; interpolation of liver boundary box in-plane to 224×224; random volumetric patch cropping (liver: 224×224×32; tumor: 128×128×32 with tumor-centered patch sampling to address class imbalance)
postprocessing: 3D connected-component labeling (largest component) after localization and after liver segmentation; voting/ensembling across 5-fold models on overlapped sub-patches; filtering tumor voxels outside segmented liver region
dataset_size: LiTS: 200 CT scans (130 train / 70 test); 3DIRCADb: 20 enhanced CT scans; LiTS liver patches 4,077 train / 1,019 validation; tumor patches 14,160 train / 3,540 validation

limitations: Long training time due to 3D convolutions requiring more parameters than 2D; false positives/negatives remain for tiny, low-contrast tumors; tumor patch size (128×128×32) chosen empirically due to computational resource limits

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: primary method is deep learning (improved 3D U-Net in a semi-supervised DCGAN), processes 3D CT volumes (256×256×16 patches), segments liver (and kidney for generalization), uses CT datasets (LiTS-2017, KiTS19), reports Dice/HD/ASSD, and presents novel contributions (SE modules + pyramid pooling in 3D U-Net; feature-restoration GAN generator for semi-supervised training). Not a framework, review, or benchmark paper.
title: Three-Dimensional Liver Image Segmentation Using Generative Adversarial Networks Based on Feature Restoration
architecture: Semi-supervised DCGAN with improved 3D U-Net as discriminator and feature-restoration DCNN as generator
architecture_details: 3D U-Net with all conv layers replaced by SE (squeeze-and-excitation) modules and a pyramid pooling module (avg-pool sizes 1, 2, 5) at the encoder end; generator restores fake 3D images from randomly selected feature maps instead of random noise; ~150M parameters
loss_function: Discriminator: sum of cross-entropy losses over labeled, unlabeled, and fake images (fake label = class 2); Generator: L2 difference between feature maps of real and fake images
preprocessing: CT value truncation/clipping to [-200, +200] HU; normalization to [0,1] using HUmax=+200, HUmin=-200; mapping to gray value [0, 255]; liver region cropped and resized to 256×256×N; cut into 256×256×16 patches
postprocessing: None mentioned
dataset_size: LiTS-2017: 100 CT scans (60 train [50 labeled/10 unlabeled], 20 val, 20 test; 500 training patches); KiTS19: 200 CT scans (1000 training patches [900 labeled/100 unlabeled], 210 val, 210 test patches)
comparison_methods: ["3D U-Net", "3D U-Net+SE+Pyramid pooling (ablation)", "DenseNet", "3D DenseUNet-65", "FCN+ACM", "GIU-Net"]
training_time: ~50 h for 100 epochs (~30 min per epoch)
limitations: Large model (~150M parameters) causing long training time (~50 h) and massive GPU memory consumption; HD/ASSD results not as strong as Dice since training was stopped based on Dice; performance below FCN+ACM and GIU-Net, attributed to limited training data; no meaningful universal quantitative metric exists to judge authenticity of GAN-generated medical images
future_work: Optimize network structure and memory efficiency to reduce training time; further improve HD/ASSD performance; develop quantitative methods for evaluating generated medical images; further study and verify general 3D image generation methods

screening_notes: Primary method is deep learning (3D U-Net backbone + Mamba SSM + VQ codebook). Processes 3D CT volumes with explicit cross-slice modeling (Mamba along z-axis at bottleneck). Segments liver (organ) jointly with liver tumors on LiTS CT — does NOT trigger the tumors-only exclusion. Reports Dice, VOE, RVD, ASD, 95HD with 3-seed mean±std, ablations, and comparisons vs 8 baselines. Novel contribution: Mamba-based global relational module, codebook quantization module, and inclusion (containment) loss. Routed as 'method' — no open-source framework/tooling claim.
title: Mamba-enhanced codebook learning with anatomical constraints for liver and tumor segmentation in 3D CT volumes
architecture: Hierarchical 3D U-Net with Mamba-based global relational module and vector-quantization codebook module
architecture_details: 3D U-Net backbone with: (1) multi-scale context encoder — three parallel branches (1x1x1+3x3x3 conv; 1x1x1 + dilated 3x3x3 simulating 5x5x5; avg-pooling branch) concatenated and fused via 1x1x1 conv; (2) codebook module — K=64 learnable prototypes, C=64 dims, nearest-neighbor assignment with straight-through estimator, commitment loss weight lambda=0.25; (3) Mamba SSM module at bottleneck (state size 16, d=64) modeling cross-slice z-axis dependencies; decoder with transposed convs, skip connections, auto center-crop/padding alignment; 1x1x1 conv output head
loss_function: L = Lseg + alpha*LVQ + beta*Lcontain (segmentation loss + VQ codebook loss + inclusion/containment loss enforcing tumors within liver); optimal alpha=0.4, beta=0.6; VQ commitment weight lambda=0.25
preprocessing: HU clipping to (-200, 200); resampling with cubic B-spline (images) and nearest-neighbor (masks), 0.5 in-plane downsampling factor, z-spacing normalized to 1 mm; random sampling of 48 liver-containing axial slices per input; min-max normalization
postprocessing: Not reported
dataset_size: LiTS: 131 training + 70 test CT scans; test-set labels withheld, so authors re-split the 131 public training scans into train/val/test
comparison_methods: ["3D U-Net", "VNet", "Att-UNet", "SegResNet", "ResUnet", "UNETR", "CodeBookUNet", "VAEUNet"]
training_time: Not reported (160 epochs, batch size 1, Adam lr=1e-4)
limitations: Validation on a single public dataset (LiTS); sharp performance drop on extremely small tumors (mean Dice < 0.05 for <10 voxel lesions); multi-scale encoder not explicitly optimized for ultra-small lesions; limited medical interpretability of codebook prototypes due to lack of subregion-level annotations in LiTS
future_work: External validation on additional multi-center cohorts (varying scanners/protocols/populations); small-lesion-aware strategies for tiny tumors; clinically grounded interpretability protocols for codebook prototypes; intermediate codebook designs to balance flexibility and generalization

screening_notes: Passes all criteria: 3D U-Net (primary), true 3D volumes (128x128x128), CT only, quantitative metrics (Dice, HD, AUC). title: Automatic renal mass segmentation and classification on CT images based on 3D U-Net and ResNet algorithms
architecture_details: Stage 1: 3D U-Net segments bilateral kidneys as ROI. Stage 2: ensemble 3D U-Net (filters=16) segments renal masses on kidney-cropped images. Classification: 10-layer 3D ResNet (pretrained weights, hidden layer=128, dropout=0.1, global average pooling + FC) classifies masses as AML/cystic/solid; Grad-CAM used for interpretability. One-stage 3D U-Net trained as ablation baseline (two-stage outperformed it).
loss_function: Not reported

postprocessing: Kidney-crop ROI extraction between cascade stages; radiodensity thresholding to remove sinus fat during KiTS21 label harmonization; no other postprocessing reported

screening_notes: Paper uses a 2D U-Net applied slice-by-slice: authors explicitly state 'Due to the complexity of Networks such as 3DSegNet or the U-Net modifications, we decided to implement the 2D-U-Net', input is 512x512 slice images, downsampling is 2D (512x512 to 16x16), and the Limitations section confirms 'A 3D semantic segmentation architecture is still not possible with the DeepLTK'. screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: 3D U-Net as primary method, true 3D processing (3D convolutions, 96x96x96 patches, full-volume aggregation), liver organ segmentation, CT modality, quantitative metrics (DSC, IoU, sensitivity, specificity, precision, accuracy, volume ratio). Novel contribution is borderline on architectural grounds (vanilla 3D U-Net with no modifications), but this is the first deep learning-based canine liver segmentation model with a newly curated veterinary CT dataset and dual-experiment evaluation, constituting a significant contribution to the field. title: Deep-learning-based automatic liver segmentation using computed tomography images in dogs

loss_function: Cross-entropy loss
preprocessing: Binary mask generation (liver=1, background=0); intensity rescaling to [-1,1] via TorchIO RescaleIntensity; volume resizing to 256x256x200 voxels (linear interpolation for images, nearest-neighbor for masks); patch extraction at 96x96x96 with 8-voxel overlap
postprocessing: Aggregation of patch-based predictions into full-volume segmentation via TorchIO GridAggregator; no additional postprocessing described

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Deep learning is the primary method (cascaded 2.5D FCNs with residual blocks); (2) Not purely 2D — the 2.5D design inputs 5 adjacent slices and outputs the middle-slice prediction, exploiting inter-slice/z-axis context, plus 3D full-connectivity and 3D dense CRF post-processing on the volume, so it does not process slices independently (borderline but passes the 'without 3D context' exclusion test); (3) Segments the liver organ (tumor is a secondary target, so exclusion #5 does not apply); (4) CT only (LiTS, 3DIRCADb contrast-enhanced CT); (5) Quantitative evaluation reported (Dice Per Case, Dice Global, IoU, VOE, RVD, ASD, RMSD); (6) Novel contributions: new boundary loss (distance+area+boundary terms), cascaded 2.5D FCN architecture, dedicated post-processing. Not a review; not a framework/tooling paper, so routed as 'method'. Minor caveat: no true 3D convolutions (2.5D approach), but volumetric context and 3D post-processing satisfy the volumetric criterion.
title: Boundary Loss-Based 2.5D Fully Convolutional Neural Networks Approach for Segmentation: A Case Study of the Liver and Tumor on Computed Tomography
architecture: Cascaded 2.5D Fully Convolutional Neural Networks (FCNs) with residual blocks
architecture_details: U-shaped encoder-decoder (similar in spirit to V-Net) implemented in 2.5D: input is 5 adjacent CT slices (H x W x 5), output is the probability map of the middle slice. Encoder blocks use residual structures (2-3 conv layers + shortcut connection, 3x3 kernels, batch norm, ReLU); symmetric decoding path restores resolution. Two-stage cascade: stage 1 segments the liver; the liver mask is dilated 5 pixels to define an ROI for stage 2 tumor segmentation.
loss_function: Stage-wise training: first combined loss Lc = w1*cross-entropy + w2*Dice (similarity coefficient) loss (w1=w2=1), then novel boundary loss Le = d + alpha*area + beta*boundary (alpha=5, beta=1) incorporating distance, area, and boundary/contour terms
preprocessing: HU truncation to [-150, 300] for liver and normalization to [0,1]; for tumor, HU truncation to [-135, 265], scaling to [0,255], grayscale reversal, then rescaling to [0,1]; data scaling augmentation 0.8-1.2x to prevent overfitting
postprocessing: Liver: 3D full connectivity to retain maximum segmentation volume, per-slice dilation. Tumor: 3D dense conditional random fields (CRFs), exclusion of false positives / false negatives with higher-than-average HU. Liver result dilated 5 iterations as ROI mask for tumor stage; liver and tumor masks merged as final output. Post-processing improved liver Dice by 5.1% and tumor Dice by 4.1%.
dataset_size: LiTS: 130 CT used for training, 70 CT for testing (dataset has 131 train/70 test); 3DIRCADb: 20 contrast-enhanced CT scans (15 liver train/5 test with cross-validation; 12 tumor train/3 test with cross-validation)

other_metrics: {"IoU_LiTS": "tumor 59.4%, liver 89.3% (2.5D FCN + boundary loss)", "VOE_RVD_ASD_RMSD": "reported on 3DIRCADb vs 2D UNet, 2D FCN, Han et al., Li et al. (table alignment partially garbled in source; e.g., tumor VOE ~57.5 +/- 13.8, ASD ~4.8 +/- 3.7 for best rows)", "false_positives": "reduced by 0.7% (liver) and 0.1% (tumor) after post-processing"}
comparison_methods: ["2D UNet (Ronneberger et al.)", "Cascaded 2D FCN (Christ et al.)", "Chlebus et al.", "3D V-Net (Milletari et al.)", "2.5D ResNet (Han et al.)", "3D H-DenseUNet (Li et al.)", "Yuan et al.", "3D AH-Net", "Med3D", "3D-DenseUNet", "Wang et al.", "Li et al. (liver, 3DIRCADb)"]
inference_time: 30-100 s total prediction time per volume, depending on number of slices; 2.5D design uses ~4 GB VRAM vs 24 GB for H-DenseUNet
