screening_notes: Criteria check: (1) DL used but only as an off-the-shelf commercial tool; the study's focus is clinical workflow/peer review, not DL methodology. (2) 3D U-Net on volumetric CT sims - met. (3) Segments OARs (bladder, anorectum) and CTV (prostate + seminal vesicles); CTV is a clinical target volume rather than a purely anatomical organ, though OARs partially satisfy this. (4) CT modality - met. (5) Reports DSC and HDmax - met. (6) Novel contribution - NOT met: no new method, architecture, training, or significant segmentation improvement; authors describe it as 'a testing methodology to assess the impact of integrating AI-based auto-contouring software into the radiotherapy contouring workflow'. Additional concerns: AI contours (C_AI) are used as the reference/'ground truth', cohorts are temporally non-comparable (42 vs. 20 patients), and no GPU/training details exist since the model is external. Triggers EXCLUDE criterion 7 ('only applies existing methods without methodological contribution'). Not a framework paper: ART-Plan is commercial closed-source software, failing F1 (open-source requirement). Borderline aspects (real quantitative DSC/HDmax on CT with a 3D U-Net) keep confidence below 0.9.
exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution: the paper evaluates the commercial, pre-trained ART-Plan software (TheraPanacea, 3D U-Net based, Class IIb medical device) explicitly stating 'no fine-tuning was performed using institutional data'. The primary contribution is a clinical radiotherapy peer-review workflow assessment (comparing manual vs. AI vs. AI-adjusted contouring), not a new segmentation method, architecture, or algorithmic improvement.

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) DL as primary method — 3D CNN (Render 3D U-Net built on 3D ANU-Net/UNet++ with attention); (2) 3D volumetric processing — 3D convolutions, maxpooling, deconvolution on 256×256×32 volume patches; (3) organ segmentation — liver, kidney, heart (not tumor-only); (4) CT modality — LiTS, KiTS, segTHOR are all CT datasets; (5) quantitative evaluation — Dice, mIoU, Recall, Hausdorff distance; (6) novel contribution — subdivision-based point-sampling replacing upsampling, FPC module, hybrid Dice+Hausdorff loss with deep supervision. No exclusion criteria triggered. Caveat: each dataset experiment is single-organ binary segmentation (one organ per task) rather than simultaneous multi-organ segmentation, so multi_organ=false.
title: Point-Sampling Method Based on 3D U-Net Architecture to Reduce the Influence of False Positive and Solve Boundary Blur Problem in 3D CT Image Segmentation
architecture_details: 3D ANU-Net (attention-based nested UNet++) encoder-decoder with dense skip connections under attention gates, deep supervision on all output blocks; subdivision-based point-sampling (overgeneration + importance/unimportance sampling of uncertain points via MLP) replaces upsampling; False Positive Classification (FPC) module (dropout, conv, adaptive maxpool, sigmoid, argmax pyramid on deepest encoder block X4_0) that blackens organ-existence predictions; Render 3D U-Net = base, with +DS and +DS+FPC ablation variants
loss_function: Hybrid loss: average over 4 deep-supervision outputs of (soft Dice loss + 0.1 × squared-error boundary term weighted by Hausdorff distance between predicted and ground-truth boundaries); binary cross entropy (BCE) for the FPC classification module
preprocessing: Unified all three datasets' volumes into patches of 256×256×32; train/test split of official training sets at 5:1 ratio
postprocessing: FPC module output gating: dot product of predicted mask with organ-existence classification {0,1} to zero-out false positive predictions (integrated module rather than standalone postprocessing)
dataset_size: 380 CT training volumes total (LiTS: 130, KiTS: 210, segTHOR: 40); split 5:1 into train/test
comparison_methods: ["3D UNet", "3D R2UNet", "3D UNet++", "Point 3D UNet++ (UNet++ + point-sampling)", "3D UNet3+", "Attention 3D UNet", "Attention 3D R2UNet"]
inference_time: ~1.6–2.0 s per 3D volume depending on task/variant (1.99 s liver, 1.68 s kidney, 1.86 s heart for full DS+FPC model)
limitations: Not explicitly stated (no dedicated limitations section); implicitly, each task segments only one organ (binary), evaluation on internal 5:1 splits of challenge training sets rather than official test servers, and modest GPU hardware limits scalability
future_work: Not explicitly stated

screening_notes: DL is primary method, CT modality, liver organ segmentation, quantitative metrics (DSC, VOE, RVD) all present — but the 3D criterion fails hard. Volume is split into 2D slices; HU windowing, histogram equalization, and flip/90°-rotation augmentation are all per-slice; architecture is a standard 2D U-Net with 3x3 convs and residual blocks. No 3D convolutions, no volumetric aggregation, no inter-slice context anywhere in the paper. That is exactly the '2D slices independently' exclusion. Novelty is also thin: ResU-Net (residual U-Net) is pre-existing; contribution is 'implementation' plus off-the-shelf preprocessing (their own wording) on 3D-IRCADb (only 20 tumor-bearing scans used). Either exclusion alone is sufficient; EX-3 is the decisive one. Note: quoted abstract DSC values (0.97%, 0.83%) are unit errors; tables report 0.9781 liver / 0.893 tumor — irrelevant since excluded.
exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context (EX-3). Secondary: applies existing ResU-Net architecture with standard preprocessing, no methodological contribution (EX-7).

screening_notes: Novel deep learning method (G-UNETR++, hybrid CNN-Transformer based on UNETR++) as primary segmentation method. Processes 3D CT volumes (3D patch embedding, 3D convolutions, volumetric input H×W×D). Segments the liver organ (not tumors) from CT. Evaluated quantitatively on three public CT datasets (LiTS, 3D-IRCADb, Sliver07) with DSC, VOE, RAVD, ASSD, MSSD, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC. Novel contributions: two gradient-based encoders using Hessian-derived second-order partial derivatives, and a hybrid Dice+CE+HD loss. No exclusion criteria met.
title: G-UNETR++: A Gradient-Enhanced Network for Accurate and Robust Liver Segmentation from Computed Tomography Images
architecture_details: Extension of UNETR++ with EPA (efficient paired attention) blocks; adds two parallel gradient-based encoders taking second-order partial derivatives (∂²f/∂x∂z and ∂²f/∂y∂z, from the last column of the Hessian matrix) as inputs to learn 3D geometric boundary features; 4-stage encoders/decoders with skip connections; deep supervision in decoder; moderate complexity (97.73M params, 73.12G FLOPs)
loss_function: Hybrid loss: Dice loss + Cross-Entropy loss + Hausdorff distance loss (equal weights α=β=γ=1), with deep supervision
preprocessing: HU value clipping to [-200, 200] to enhance liver contrast; resize CT slices from 512×512 to 256×256; data augmentation (scaling, rotation, mirroring, intensity shifting); five-fold cross-validation
postprocessing: Connected components algorithm (retain largest connected region) + median filter to remove noise
dataset_size: 171 CT scans total: 131 (LiTS; split 91 train / 20 val / 20 test), 20 (3D-IRCADb), 20 (Sliver07)
comparison_methods: ["UNETR++ (baseline)", "TransUNet", "UNETR", "Swin-UNETR", "nnFormer", "FCN+ACM", "MA-Net", "S-Net+T-Net+SEL+PRL", "DefED-Net", "HDU-Net", "HFRU-Net", "DHT-Net", "CotepRes-Net", "DRAUNet", "U-Net", "mU-Net", "EDCNN", "RMAU-Net"]
gpu_used: 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GB each); Xeon w3-2435 CPU, 128 GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04
training_time: Not mentioned (trained 1000 epochs, batch size 64, Adam optimizer, initial LR 5e-4)
limitations: G-Encoders increase complexity vs UNETR++ (97.73M vs 42.96M params; 73.12G vs 47.98G FLOPs); false positives near adjacent organs (stomach, spleen, heart) due to overlapping intensity values; false negatives in small regions near tumor boundaries
future_work: Reduce model complexity via multi-resolution second-order derivative computation on ROIs and adaptive activation of gradient-enhanced encoders; extend to other organs (abdominal multi-organ) and modalities beyond CT (MRI)

screening_notes: Meets most criteria: deep learning is the primary method (2D FCN, 2D U-Net in TensorFlow); CT modality; segments organs (liver, kidney, spleen); reports quantitative Dice (best liver 0.9789 mean with FCN); presents a novel contribution (pre-training-based hard/easy sample balancing for data augmentation). Fails inclusion criterion 2 / triggers exclusion rule 3: the networks operate on individual 2D slices independently; although data come from 3D CT volumes and results are visualized in 3D, there is no 3D context or volumetric processing in the method itself. Borderline because the data balancing operates at volume level, hence confidence 0.9 not 1.0.
exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context. The paper explicitly adopts a 'classical 2D FCN model based on VGG-16 and 2D U-Net' and performs slice-by-slice training/classification with no 3D convolutions or inter-slice/volumetric context mechanism.

screening_notes: Paper meets all other criteria: (1) deep learning (U-Net-derived CNN with Squeeze-and-Excitation connections, pyramid structure, auto-context cascade) is the primary method; (2) segments multiple anatomical organs (13 head-and-neck OARs: eyes, temporal lobes, mandibles, brainstem, parotids, submandibular glands, spinal cord, thyroid; plus liver on LiTS); (3) CT modality (private NPC head-and-neck CT dataset, 356 patients; LiTS public CT); (4) quantitative evaluation (Dice, Dice per case/global, precision, recall, 5-fold cross-validation; best mean Dice 83.28% on NPC OARs, liver Dice 85.47% per case on LiTS); (5) novel contribution (SEC skip-connection module, pyramid fusion, cascaded auto-context). However, the method is strictly 2D slice-wise — images resized to 256×256 and processed slice-by-slice — which fails the review's core 3D/volumetric requirement. Note: paper is otherwise a borderline-relevant 'method' study that reviewers of the full corpus may wish to flag as 2D-only OAR segmentation in CT.
exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criterion 2 (3D/Volumetric): the paper explicitly uses 2D networks processing CT slices independently, corresponding to exclusion criterion 3 (only 2D slices without 3D context). The authors state: 'each slice is one training sample in a 2D network' and 'Based on these above reasons, we decided to use 2D networks in our experiments' — they tested the 2.5D H-DenseUNet but rejected it due to GPU memory limits (batch size 1), with no 3D convolutions or inter-slice/volumetric context anywhere in the architecture.

screening_notes: Meets criteria 1 (CNN primary), 4 (CT), 5 (Dice/IoU/AUC reported), and arguably 6 (two-stage successive encoder-decoder). Fails criterion 2 decisively: architecture tables show 2D feature maps throughout (encoder input 256^2 x 1, per-slice processing, no 3D convolutions, no volumetric context). Explicit statement: 'Photoshop CC 2018 was used to achieve the 3D volume reconstruction of liver tumor' from adjacent 2D segmentation maps. Liver Dice 0.92, tumor Dice 0.75 on LiTS+KCGMH (4300 images).
exclusion_reason: Fails S3 criterion 3: processes 2D slices independently without 3D context. SED-1 (U-Net) and SED-2 (FC-DenseNet) take single-channel 256x256x1 2D slice inputs with 2D convolutions/pooling (Tables 1-2); the '3D' in the title is only post-hoc tumor contour reconstruction performed in Photoshop CC 2018 for visualization, not volumetric or 3D-convolutional processing. Secondary concern: the primary target is liver lesion/tumor segmentation; liver segmentation (SED-1) serves as a ROI pre-processing stage for tumor extraction (borderline vs. S3-EXCL-5).

screening_notes: Retraction is explicit in title, watermark, and publisher note ('This paper has been retracted'). Even setting retraction aside: deep learning is primary (GAN + YOLOv3-ResNet-50 + DeepLabv3/InceptionResNetV2), CT modality (3D-IRCADb), liver organ + liver tumor segmented, and quantitative metrics reported (IoU 0.99, F1 0.995, accuracy) — but no Dice is reported, '3D' processing is slice-based, and much of the evaluation centers on tumor localization/segmentation. Retraction is decisive; no extraction performed.
exclusion_reason: Retracted paper — retraction notice published 26 August 2026 (Diagnostics 2026, 16, 2728). Retracted publications are ineligible for systematic review inclusion. Secondary concern: despite '3D-semantic segmentation' branding, the pipeline operates on 2D slices (GAN input 64x64x3, segmentation input 512x512x3; no 3D convolutions described), so criterion 2 (volumetric 3D processing) is not credibly met.

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) DL is primary method (3D U-Net, Res U-Net, SegNet, DeepLabV3+, UNETR); (2) 3D/volumetric processing - pipeline operates on 3D cubes (1x96x192x192 stage 1; 1x64x160x160 stage 2) with 3D convolutions/max-pooling/up-convolutions; (3) segments kidney (organ), plus kidney stones; (4) unenhanced abdominal CT; (5) quantitative metrics reported (Dice, specificity, sensitivity, accuracy); (6) novel contribution via proposed two-stage coarse-to-fine training scheme showing significant improvement over independently trained models, plus first open-source annotated kidney+kidney-stone unenhanced CT dataset (Zenodo). Not excluded by criterion 7 since the two-stage replaceable training scheme constitutes a methodological contribution, not just application of existing methods. Note: partially targets stones (lesions) but organ (kidney) segmentation is central, so exclusion criterion 5 does not apply.
title: Deep Segmentation Networks for Segmenting Kidneys and Detecting Kidney Stones in Unenhanced Abdominal CT Images
architecture: Two-stage coarse-to-fine training scheme with replaceable segmentation networks: 3D U-Net, Res U-Net, SegNet, DeepLabV3+, UNETR (best: Res U-Net)
architecture_details: Stage 1: coarse kidney segmentation on clipped 3D cubes (1, 96, 192, 192) with whole region center-cropped to (1, z, 192, 192); Stage 2: fine kidney + kidney stone segmentation on cubes (1, 64, 160, 160) cropped per kidney from Stage 1 predictions; Res U-Net combines residual units with U-Net skip connections; UNETR uses transformer encoder with U-shaped decoder; DeepLabV3+ uses Xception backbone with ASPP
loss_function: Combined Dice + cross-entropy loss; AdamW optimizer (weight decay 0.001), ReduceLROnPlateau with initial LR 0.001, 200 epochs, batch size 8
preprocessing: HU intensity clipping to [-135, 215]; z-axis spacing resampled to 1.25 mm (native range 0.42-2.5 mm); min-max normalization of HU; center cropping on x/y axes (256x256 stage 1; 512x512 stage 2); 3D cube clipping with regionprops-based region analysis (stage 1: length 96, stride 48; stage 2: length 64, stride 32)
postprocessing: Stage 1 coarse mask resampled to original resolution; per-kidney 3D cube cropping based on stage 1 predictions; predicted kidney and kidney stone masks overlaid on final output image
datasets: ["In-house unenhanced abdominal CT dataset from First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University (260 scans, open-access at https://zenodo.org/record/6042410)"]
dataset_size: 260 unenhanced abdominal CT scans (209 with stones, 51 without); 7:3 train/test split with 5-fold cross-validation
dice_per_organ: {"kidney": "96.54 +/- 1.06% (Res U-Net, proposed scheme); 3D U-Net 96.05 +/- 1.68%; SegNet 95.04 +/- 1.18%; UNETR 93.35 +/- 1.45%; DeepLabV3+ 81.73 +/- 2.43%; independent training best: 3D U-Net 96.70%, Res U-Net 95.81%", "kidney_stone": "80.59 +/- 1.28% (Res U-Net, proposed scheme); 3D U-Net 80.04 +/- 1.75%; SegNet 75.59 +/- 2.23%; UNETR 74.36 +/- 0.80%; DeepLabV3+ 33.36 +/- 3.17%; independent training best: Res U-Net 79.83%, 3D U-Net 77.63%; by stone size (Res U-Net proposed): small 60.11 +/- 0.84, middle 76.08 +/- 3.46, large 83.39 +/- 2.33"}
other_metrics: {"specificity": "99.99 +/- 0.01% (Res U-Net, proposed scheme, kidney and stone)", "sensitivity": "kidney 96.49 +/- 0.08%, kidney stone 79.73 +/- 1.90% (Res U-Net, proposed scheme)", "accuracy": "99.95% (Res U-Net, independent training)", "success_rate": "Reported as bar-chart figures for kidney and stone segmentation success rates (dependent vs independent training)"}
comparison_methods: ["3D U-Net", "Res U-Net", "SegNet", "DeepLabV3+", "UNETR", "independent one-step training (ablation vs proposed two-stage dependent training)", "stone-size-stratified analysis (small/middle/large)"]
gpu_used: NVIDIA Tesla A100 with 40 GB VRAM (server: 64 GB RAM, 2.15 GHz AMD EPYC 7742 CPU)
limitations: Two-stage scheme requires heavy computing resources; stage 2 depends on stage 1 outputs, so a false positive can affect kidney region cropping and lead to incorrect predictions; kidney stone detection remains difficult due to varying sizes, appearance diversity, small shapes, and many negative samples; DeepLabV3+ and UNETR performed unsatisfactorily, particularly on stones
future_work: Develop a single segmentation network that avoids the two-stage dependency without sacrificing fine segmentation quality; annotate and segment inner kidney structures using enhanced CT images; extend techniques to preoperative planning for percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) surgical intervention

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) nnU-Net DNN is the primary segmentation method (DOKEN is a domain-knowledge preprocessing/auto-labeling step feeding the DNN); (2) 3D volumetric CT processing (3D erosion-dilation parsing, 3D digital heart models, voxel-spacing resampling); (3) segments left atrium + 4 pulmonary veins + LA appendage (cardiac organ substructures, not tumors); (4) cardiac CT modality; (5) quantitative metrics reported (Dice 96.7%, surface distance 1.51 mm, centroid-boundary distance); (6) novel contribution via DOKEN label-efficient training paradigm (train:test ratio 1:5). Not a review, not a tooling/platform paper. Note: multi_organ set to false since all six structures belong to a single organ (heart/LA complex).

screening_notes: Passes criteria 1-5 nominally: deep learning segmentation (image-to-image network + conditional VAE per ref [9]), 3D CT volumes, cardiac chamber/myocardium segmentation, non-contrast chest CT, quantitative evaluation (ICC, Bland-Altman — though no overlap metrics like Dice/Hausdorff are reported, only volume agreement). Fails criterion 6/EXCLUDE-7: no methodological contribution; model predates the study and was developed by Siemens Healthineers. This is a clinical application/validation paper, not a methods paper. Not a framework paper (closed, research-only commercial tool, no versioned release or benchmark reproduction).
exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution. The paper is a clinical validation study of an existing, previously published deep learning model (Siemens AI-Rad Companion Research; architecture described in Jacob et al. 2023, ref [9]). The authors explicitly state the objective was to 'assess the accuracy of an existing deep learning model' and that 'algorithm development was done independently from and finalized prior to the results presented in this manuscript.' No new method, architecture, or improvement is presented.

screening_notes: Clinical validation/comparison study (86 contrast-enhanced abdominal CTs, single center). Meets CT (criterion 4), organ (liver, criterion 3), and metric (Dice 0.911-0.946, HD, Bland-Altman, criterion 5) requirements, but fails novelty (criterion 6): both DL tools are cited prior work (ref [15] R-Vessel-X, ref [16] TotalSegmentator) run as-is. No model is trained, modified, or improved. Also arguably fails criterion 1 (DL as primary method) since the paper is an agreement/efficiency study across manual, semi-automatic, and automatic approaches. Not a framework paper itself; it is a user of TotalSegmentator/RVX.
exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution (exclusion criterion 7): the paper benchmarks off-the-shelf tools (RVX Semi-Automatic, RVX Deep Learning, TotalSegmentator in 3D Slicer) against manual segmentation. No new architecture, training, or method is developed; deep learning is an evaluated tool, not the paper's primary method (criterion 2).

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) DL primary (3D U-Net, VGG-16); (2) 3D U-Net processes volumetric CT via 64x64x64 3D patches (VGG-16 arm is 2D axial, but the 3D arm satisfies criterion); (3) organ segmentation (liver, pancreas, left atrium); (4) CT used (LiTS, MSD liver/pancreas) — note the MSD cardiac arm is MRI, but CT datasets dominate; (5) eight quantitative metrics incl. Dice, HD, AUC; (6) contribution = systematic parametric study proposing best init/loss/optimizer/activation combinations with paired t-tests. Borderline on novelty (no new architecture, existing networks re-applied), but the combinatorial evaluation with statistical significance testing qualifies as a methodological contribution rather than 'only applying existing methods'. Internal paper inconsistency: abstract attributes VGG-16 results to LiTS, Section 3.7 says SLIVER07. Classified 'method': not a framework/tooling paper, not a survey, not a dataset/challenge paper.

screening_notes: Novel dual-headed multitask U-Net (FG-CKD-UNet) for kidney compartment segmentation (cortex/medulla/pelvis) plus eGFR prediction with a structure-function consistency loss. DL is the primary method, the kidney is an organ, quantitative metrics are reported (Dice 0.94, HD95 9.8 mm), and the contribution is novel — so it passes criteria 1, 3, 5, 6. However, it fails the 3D/volumetric requirement: the architecture, equations, and preprocessing all operate on 2D slices (H×W×C inputs, 3×3 kernels, pixel-wise metrics, volumetric biomarkers computed by summing over 2D indices i,j). The 'kidney volume' biomarker is therefore not true volumetric analysis of a 3D CT volume. Regarding CT modality: the only CT data is a colorized 2D kidney image classification dataset (Normal/Cyst/Tumor/Stone) with no segmentation masks, used solely as an external evaluation set; the authors explicitly state that all segmentation learning, biomarker extraction, and eGFR prediction were trained and evaluated only on the T2-weighted MRI dataset. For a review on 3D organ segmentation from CT, this paper's primary modality is MRI and its processing is 2D, so it is excluded.
exclusion_reason: Fails Include Criterion 2 / triggers Exclude Criterion 3: the model processes 2D slices independently with no 3D context (input defined as X ∈ R^{H×W×C}, 2D 3×3 convolutions, pixel-accuracy metrics, 2D Euclidean distance transform, CT images resized to 150×150 px 2D colorized images, batching of 'MRI slices' and 'CT images'). Additionally triggers Exclude Criterion 4: the core segmentation and eGFR prediction task is trained and evaluated exclusively on T2-weighted MRI; the colorized CT dataset (12,446 label-free 2D images) is used only for external cross-modality robustness checks with no CT segmentation ground truth.

screening_notes: Otherwise strong candidate: novel deep learning architecture (FF-ResUNet, a skip-free collaborative residual U-Net) as primary method; segments liver (organ) + tumors on CT (LiTS, 3D-IRCADb, AMOS-CT); reports quantitative metrics (Dice 0.952 liver / 0.737 tumor, HD95, communication payload); clear methodological contribution (privacy-preserving split-learning design, multi-scale dilated decoder, boundary-aware loss, ablations). It satisfies criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 but unambiguously fails the 3D/volumetric requirement, so it is excluded despite its quality. Also note it is not a framework/tooling paper (no open-source platform release), so study-type routing would have been 'method' if included.
exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criterion 2 (3D/Volumetric) and triggers exclusion criterion 3: the paper explicitly adopts a 2D slice-based formulation — input is a single axial slice (256×256×1), all baselines were 'trained using 2D axial slices', and the authors state 3D context was intentionally avoided to reduce communication overhead. No 3D convolutions, 2.5D multi-view inputs, or inter-slice context are used; volumetric resampling (1mm³) is only preprocessing.

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) deep learning (CNN/UNet family) is the primary segmentation method; (2) true 3D/volumetric processing - 3D convolutions applied to whole CT volumes resized to 128x128x128, explicitly contrasted with 2D slice-based approaches; (3) segments lung organ (binary) plus lung+infection regions (multi-class) - infection is included but lung organ segmentation is the core task, so exclude-criterion-5 does not apply; (4) CT modality; (5) quantitative metrics reported (Dice, IoU, accuracy); (6) methodological contribution via novel 3D UNet encoder modifications (3D ResNet152/3D VGG19/3D DenseNet201 backbones with/without ImageNet transfer learning). Not a review, not framework tooling. Caveats: very small dataset (20 CT scans), contributions are incremental backbone substitutions, and provided text is truncated before full results/limitations sections, so per-variant result tables and stated limitations could not be extracted.
title: Lung and Infection CT-Scan-Based Segmentation with 3D UNet Architecture and Its Modification
architecture: 3D UNet plus three modified variants: 3D ResUNet, 3D VGGUNet, 3D DenseUNet
architecture_details: 3D UNet (encoder: conv blocks with batch norm + ReLU + max pooling; decoder: upconvolution with skip concatenation; dropout layers added to conv blocks for regularization). Encoder replaced by 3D ResNet152 (3D ResUNet), 3D VGG19 (3D VGGUNet), or 3D DenseNet201 (3D DenseUNet); each modified variant trained with and without ImageNet transfer learning on the encoder, yielding seven models per segmentation case.

postprocessing: 3D projection of segmented infection output for severity visualization; no other explicit postprocessing described (3D approach chosen partly to simplify postprocessing vs 2D)

limitations: Not stated in provided text (article truncated before Discussion/Conclusion). Implicit limitations: very small dataset (20 CT scans), higher computational cost of 3D vs 2D architectures acknowledged, original 3D UNet required more iterations to reach maximum results.
future_work: Not stated in provided text; paper emphasizes clinical use of 3D infection projections for COVID-19 severity assessment (mild/moderate/severe) as the application benefit.

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: primary method is 3D U-Net (MONAI/PyTorch) with a novel anatomy-guided naïve Bayes soft-label integration (first automated CT pancreatic subregion segmentation method); processes 3D CT volumes explicitly (argues 2D is unsuitable); CT-only (contrast-enhanced abdominal CT; NIH + 2 in-house sets); quantitative DSC reported per fold and per subregion; clear novelty via multistage anatomy-guided framework. Confidence held at 0.85 because it segments pancreatic subregions (head/body/tail) within a pre-delineated pancreas rather than segmenting the whole organ from raw CT — not tumor/lesion-only, so exclusion criterion 5 does not apply, but whole-pancreas segmentation is declared out of scope. Study type: method (MONAI is merely used as backend, not presented as a framework contribution).
title: Segmentation of Pancreatic Subregions in Computed Tomography Images
architecture: Multistage anatomy-guided 3D U-Net with naïve Bayes soft-label integration
architecture_details: Conventional 3D U-Net (Çiçek et al.) with 3 down-sampling and 3 up-sampling steps; naïve Bayes model (length + volumetric anatomical features) generates per-voxel soft-label probability maps; U-Net output is updated each epoch to the joint probability of U-Net and Bayes maps (renormalized per pixel). Implemented in MONAI 0.7 with PyTorch 1.8.0; Bayes model in MATLAB 2021b. Input: cropped pancreas volume with normalized intensities + subregional labels as second channel.
loss_function: Mean Dice loss + focal loss at 1:1 ratio (per subregion)
preprocessing: Cropped to pancreas region using reference labels to fixed 218×239×288 (x,y,z); non-pancreas voxels set to 0; pancreas voxel intensities normalized to 0–1 by linear scaling; no other preprocessing
postprocessing: None reported (joint probability map normalization is performed within the model pipeline)
datasets: ["NIH Pancreas-CT (public, healthy pancreas)", "D1 (in-house CSMC, pre-cancerous pancreas)", "D2 (in-house CSMC, cancerous pancreas)"]
dataset_size: 112 CT scans total: 82 NIH + 15 D1 + 15 D2 (all contrast-enhanced abdominal CT; D1/D2 predominantly portal venous phase)
other_metrics: {"DSC_formula": "2TP/(2TP+FP+FN)", "mean_DSC_improvement_from_Bayes_integration": "~8% across all three datasets", "inter_grader_label_overlap": "84% initial, 96% after review"}
comparison_methods: ["3D U-Net without Bayes soft-label integration (ablation baseline)", "No external method comparison (first method for this task; compared against manually created benchmark labels)"]
training_time: ~8 h on 60 training 3D volumes; max 500 epochs (converged ~200), batch size 2, Adam optimizer, lr 1e-4, 4-fold cross-validation
limitations: Assumes a complete pancreas; may fail after surgical interventions (pancreatectomy, Whipple) or when subregion sizes vary due to disorders (e.g., inflammation); relies on a pre-delineated whole-pancreas mask (whole pancreas segmentation out of scope); trained/validated on small datasets; most failures (~67%) occur at the body/tail border and in U-shaped pancreatic morphology
future_work: Extend model to MR images; train on larger datasets with high textural variation (pancreatitis, pancreatic cysts); explore Tversky loss for difficult cases

screening_notes: The paper otherwise meets most criteria: deep learning is the primary method (hybrid ViT encoder + ASPP + attention-gated U-Net-like decoder, 136M params; LAURA variants down to ~5M), input is CT (MSD Task 06 Lung, NSCLC-Radiogenomics; 307 cases), quantitative metrics are extensively reported (Dice, Sensitivity, Specificity, GFLOPs, VRAM, inference time, statistical tests), and there is a clear novel contribution (new hybrid architecture plus federated learning framework with FedProx, adaptive weighted aggregation, dynamic virtual clients; best centralized Dice 84.24% on MSD Lung). However, exclusion is unambiguous: the title itself states '2D Hybrid Transformer', all convolutions are Conv2d with 256x256 single-slice inputs, the authors contrast their approach with 3D architectures like nnU-Net/UNETR, and the segmentation target is lung tumor rather than an anatomical organ. The federated-learning 'framework' framing does not qualify it as a tooling/platform paper (not MONAI/nnInteractive-style).
exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criteria 2 (3D/Volumetric) and 3 (Organ Segmentation). (a) The method operates on individual 2D axial slices only: '3D CT scans are preprocessed into 256 × 256 2D axial slices' with 'only axial slices containing the tumor... extracted', and the authors explicitly acknowledge 'the current framework's reliance on 2D slice processing... at the expense of ignoring critical volumetric context', deferring a 2.5D extension to future work (exclusion criterion 3: only processes 2D slices without 3D context; is_3d = false). (b) The paper segments lung TUMORS/lesions, not anatomical organs — 'automatic lung tumor segmentation' (exclusion criterion 5: only segments tumors/lesions, not organs).

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Deep learning (3D U-Net with attention gates) is the primary method; (2) fully volumetric 3D processing (3x3x3 convolutions, 3D max-pooling, 224x224x128 volume input); (3) segments the pancreas organ (binary segmentation, MSD tumor labels merged into organ mask); (4) CT modality only (NIH and MSD pancreas CT datasets); (5) quantitative metrics reported (DSC, ASSD, HD95 with 5-fold CV + held-out test); (6) novel contribution is borderline but sufficient: custom attention-gate implementation with Layer Normalization and C/2 reduction, systematic loss-function ablation (Dice vs Dice+CE vs Dice+Focal) with Friedman statistical testing, showing significant improvement over their own 3D U-Net baseline (80.8% vs 77.6% on NIH) and competitive results with reported variance/range, which prior compared works lack. Not a review, not a framework/tooling paper, not a benchmark/challenge paper.
title: Deep Learning Model with Attention Mechanism for a 3D Pancreas Segmentation in CT Scans
authors: Idriss Cabrel Tsewalo Tondji et al.
architecture: 3D Attention U-Net (3D U-Net encoder-decoder with attention gates at skip connections)
architecture_details: Symmetric encoder-decoder with 4 downsampling blocks (two 3x3x3 convolutions each, batch normalization, ReLU, 3D max-pooling stride 2); feature channels 2->16 in deepest encoder layer, mirrored 16->2 in decoder with 3D transposed convolutions; attention gates at every skip connection using 1x1x1 convolutions, Layer Normalization, a two-layer subnetwork with C/2 reduction channels and sigmoid-activated voxel-wise attention maps
loss_function: Dice + Focal loss (total = L_Dice + L_Focal); ablated against Dice-only and Dice+CrossEntropy, with Dice+Focal significantly better than Dice-only (Friedman test, post-hoc p=0.03 on both datasets)
preprocessing: HU windowing to [-100, 240]; min-max normalization to [0,1]; resampling to 1.0x1.0x1.0 mm3 isotropic spacing; fixed center cropping to 224x224x128 voxels (mask-independent, to avoid label leakage); for MSD, pancreas+tumor labels merged into a single binary mask; 3D on-the-fly augmentation (random rotations +/-10 deg, random flips p=0.5, random shifts up to 10%)
postprocessing: None mentioned
datasets: ["NIH Healthy Pancreas-CT Dataset (TCGA/cancerimagingarchive)", "Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) Pancreas Dataset"]
dataset_size: NIH: 81-82 abdominal CT scans (65 in 5-fold CV + 16 held-out test; 2 scans excluded for missing masks); MSD: 281 CT scans (230 in 5-fold CV + 51 held-out test)
comparison_methods: ["3D U-Net (own baseline, 77.6% DSC NIH)", "Bharat/Giddwani et al. Deep Dilated V-Net (83.31%)", "Boers et al. Interactive 3D U-Net (78.10%)", "Jain et al. cascaded 3D approach (81.75%)", "Li et al. meta-learning approach (80.24% MSD)", "Zhang et al. multi-atlas + level-set (82.47% MSD)", "Chen et al. two-view feature learning (76.60% MSD)"]

inference_time: 2.75 s per case (NIH); 2.72 s per case (MSD)
limitations: Experiments conducted on datasets of limited size and heterogeneity, constraining robustness of learned representations; model may be sensitive to anatomical variability of pancreas shape/appearance; generalization to out-of-distribution samples remains limited and requires validation on more diverse clinical cohorts
future_work: Incorporate larger multi-center datasets for cross-dataset generalization experiments to assess robustness to domain shift; extend pipeline to tumor segmentation building on the automated pancreas segmentation, with the goal of imaging-based prognosis prediction

screening_notes: Borderline case that meets all other criteria: deep learning is the primary method (attention U-Net with GN); CT modality (SegTHOR, StructSeg 2019); organ segmentation (esophagus as OAR, though multi-class models output all thoracic OARs); quantitative metrics reported (Dice, HD/HD95); clear novel contribution (spatial attention decoder, group normalization, STAPLE-based k-fold fusion) with state-of-the-art claims (Dice 0.8690 on SegTHOR test via leaderboard; 0.7784 on StructSeg training set, outperforming SCSE/CBAM variants and MTL-WMCE). The sole disqualifying factor is the 2D/3D criterion: the network processes each slice independently with zero 3D operations. The volumetric elements present (slice extraction from 3D volumes, 3D reconstruction of outputs, STAPLE fusion on reconstructed volumes, 3D Dice/HD evaluation via challenge leaderboard, 3D visualization in Fig. 4) were considered but judged insufficient to constitute '3D context' in segmentation decisions, as no inter-slice information informs the model's predictions. Reviewers seeking to include 2D/2.5D slice-based pipelines evaluated on 3D volumes could reasonably include this paper, hence moderate confidence.
exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criterion 2 (3D/Volumetric) and meets exclusion criterion 3 (only processes 2D slices without 3D context). The method is a purely 2D U-Net variant (2D convolutions with 3x3/1x1 kernels, ImageNet-pretrained 2D backbones ResNet34/SEResNext50) applied independently to slices extracted from CT volumes. The authors explicitly state the method 'is based on the processing of slice images from the original three-dimensional (3D) image so that our method does not require large computational resources' and that they 'used 2D images for training to save a massive amount of computing resources compared to 3D volumes'. No 3D convolutions or inter-slice volumetric context are used in the segmentation model; STAPLE is ensemble label-fusion post-processing across k-fold checkpoints, not volumetric segmentation context.

screening_notes: Novel deep learning method (DG-TTA: GIN augmentation + SSC descriptor + consistency-based test-time adaptation, integrated into nnUNet). Explicitly 3D (volumetric nnUNet models, 1.5mm isotropic resampling, stated advantage over 2D-only competitors). Segments abdominal organs, spine, and cardiac structures from CT source domains (BTCV, AMOS-CT, TotalSegmentator, MMWHS-CT) cross-domain to MRI. Reports Dice and HD95 with significance tests. Study type: method — code repo exists but the paper's contribution is an algorithm, not an open-source framework/tooling platform, so framework routing does not apply.
title: DG-TTA: Out-of-Domain Medical Image Segmentation Through Augmentation, Descriptor-Driven Domain Generalization, and Test-Time Adaptation
architecture_details: nnUNet with domain-generalized pre-training (GIN intensity augmentation + SSC self-similarity context descriptor input) and test-time adaptation via two-branch augmented consistency self-supervision; variants evaluated: standard nnUNet, nnUNet with batch norm layers (partial-layer adaptation ablations: norm-only, encoder-only); three-fold TTA ensemble at inference; AdamW (lr 1e-5, wd 0.01), 12 optimization steps, gradient accumulation over 16 patches
loss_function: Soft Dice loss for TTA consistency between two spatially augmented branches (d=2 exponent); supervised nnUNet training loss for pre-training
preprocessing: Resampling to uniform 1.50x1.50x1.50 mm3 voxels; GIN (global intensity non-linear) augmentation via randomly re-initialized shallow conv net blended with input; SSC descriptor (6-neighborhood patch-distance based, patch size/distance 1 voxel) applied to network input; for TS>SPINE, TS ground truth cropped to exclude spinous processes via 5-voxel dilated mask
postprocessing: Prediction correction to match label definitions (e.g., removing spinous processes for spine evaluation); ensemble of three TTA model folds in final nnUNet inference; consistency masking of inverse-transform border artifacts during TTA
dataset_size: 5 public datasets: BTCV 30 abdominal CT (20 train/10 test); AMOS 500 CT + 100 MR; TotalSegmentator 1204 CT (600 sampled for training); MyoSegmenTUM 54 MR; MMWHS 60 CT + 60 MR (12 CT train / 6 MR test); CT(source) > MR(target) cross-domain scenarios

screening_notes: Passes all criteria: DL is primary method (SwinUNETR ViT + modified 3D UNet); processes 3D volumes (SwinUNETR on 128^3 patches, tumor UNet patch 192x128x128); segments kidney organ (Dice 0.97) in addition to tumors, so not tumor-only; CECT modality; quantitative metrics reported (Dice, sensitivity, FPC, precision, VD, OSR, USR); novel contribution via dual-stage pipeline with residual blocks + attention gates and improved small-tumor sensitivity. Not a framework paper - no open-source tooling released.
title: Dual-Stage AI Model for Enhanced CT Imaging: Precision Segmentation of Kidney and Tumors
architecture: Dual-stage: SwinUNETR (ViT-based) for kidney segmentation + enhanced 3D UNet (Kidney Tumor 3D UNet) for tumor detection/segmentation
architecture_details: Stage 1: SwinUNETR with shifted-window transformer, non-overlapping 128^3 patches, 4-stage encoder (2 transformer blocks each), CNN decoder with residual blocks, 3D convs, instance normalization, AdamW lr=3.5e-4, pretrained weights. Stage 2: nnUNet-3D-enhanced 6-stage encoder with ResNet-style residual blocks (1,3,4,6,6,6), attention gates, LeakyReLU, SGD lr=0.001, patch 192x128x128, batch 5; VOI from stage 1 expanded 25%
loss_function: DiceCE (Dice + cross-entropy) for both stages
preprocessing: HU clipping to 0.5-99.5 percentile range, isotropic resampling to 1.0 mm voxel spacing, intensity normalization (zero mean, unit variance); augmentation: random rotations, scaling, mirroring, axis transposition, gamma correction (+5.5% Dice)
postprocessing: None reported
dataset_size: 1081 CECT scans (KiTS23: 489 = 389 train / 100 internal validation; private: 592 external validation)
comparison_methods: ["nnUNet-3D (single-stage and dual-stage)", "SwinUNETR (single-stage and dual-stage)"]
limitations: Private dataset lacks benign tumor/cyst annotations, causing some FP cyst detections; private test set limited to ccRCC subtype only, limiting generalization across RCC subtypes
future_work: Hybrid CNN-ViT models with optimal layer fusion; single recursive network for both organ and tumor segmentation; larger datasets with more diverse RCC subtypes

screening_notes: All inclusion criteria met: deep learning (residual 3D U-Net) is the primary segmentation method; operates on 3D CT volumes (96x96x96 patches); segments spleen on abdominal CT (portal venous phase); reports DSC, Hausdorff, ASSD, RAVD. Novel contribution is not architectural (uses MONAI's standard residual U-Net) but is a controlled evaluation: curates a novel pathological-spleen dataset and cross-tests against an MSD-trained model, demonstrating training-set composition drives robustness (DSC 0.941 vs 0.648, p<0.001) - a substantive empirical contribution, not a mere application. Not a framework paper: MONAI is used as tooling, not presented/evaluated as the contribution (F1 fails), so routed to 'method' by elimination (not a survey, not a dataset/challenge paper). Minor data quality note: reported split percentages (32.52%/9.15%/20.33%) sum to ~62%, likely a reporting error in the source.
title: Evaluation of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Automated Spleen Segmentation in Patients with Conditions Directly or Indirectly Affecting the Spleen
architecture_details: Enhanced U-Net with residual units as described by Kerfoot et al., implemented in MONAI v0.5.0; encode path uses strided convolutions, decode path uses strided transpose convolutions, with skip connections; trained for 500 epochs, batch size 2, Adam optimizer, learning rate 1e-4
loss_function: Dice loss
preprocessing: DICOM to NIfTI conversion; resampling to 1.5x1.5x2.0 mm voxels (bilinear for images, nearest-neighbor for masks); intensity windowing/clipping to -57 to 164 HU; random cropping to 96x96x96 voxel patches with balanced positive/negative sampling ratio
postprocessing: Sigmoid activation; stitching of separately processed patches; binarization at threshold 0.5; resampling to original scan resolution; retention of largest connected component; Laplace edge detection for contour visualization
datasets: ["In-house Charité dataset (portal venous phase abdominal CT)", "Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) Spleen task"]
dataset_size: 122 CT scans total (61 in-house + 61 MSD); each split into training/validation/test (reported as 32.52%/9.15%/20.33%; in-house: 41 train+val / 20 test; MSD: 41 train+val / 20 test)
comparison_methods: ["Open U-Net (same architecture trained on MSD)", "Gauriau et al. (template deformation)", "Wood et al. (ML + 3D active contours)", "Gloger et al. (shape priors, MRI)", "Gibson et al. (dense V-networks)", "Linguraru et al. (atlas-based)"]
framework: PyTorch 1.8.1 with MONAI 0.5.0 and PyTorch Lightning 0.9.0 (Python 3.7)
limitations: Small in-house dataset (n=61, chosen to match MSD size) vs. 250-450 scans in comparable works; no cross-validation performed; trained/validated only on portal venous phase CT (may not generalize to other acquisition protocols); complex intrasplenic distortions (infarctions, focal lesions) excluded, creating preselection bias risk
future_work: GAN-based data augmentation to compensate for low incidence of rare splenic conditions; transfer learning to avoid time/energy-intensive retraining; clinical evaluation of the algorithm for quantitative imaging biomarkers (e.g., differentiating causes of splenomegaly, assessing cirrhosis/portal hypertension)

screening_notes: Passes all inclusion criteria: DL is the primary automatic method (DeepMedic, NiftyNet, four U-Net variants; DL methods rank top-4 and outperform all semi-automatic baselines); volumetric evaluation on 3D contrast-enhanced abdominal CT (DeepMedic is a 3D CNN; NiftyNet volumetric; METU_U-Net 2D with adjacent-slice 3D context); organ segmentation (liver in transplant donors); quantitative metrics reported (VO/Dice-equivalent, RVD, ASSD, RMSD, MSSD); novel contribution (ITU_U-Net and METU_U-Net introduced for the first time, plus challenge evaluation setup and ensemble/MV/STAPLE fusion analysis). Not tumor-only, not a survey. Routed as 'benchmark': the paper is fundamentally a challenge paper (annotation framework, dataset release to teams, unified evaluation of 12 participant methods, semi-automatic baselines) rather than a pure method paper; the novel U-Nets are challenge entries. Not a framework paper (NiftyNet/DeepMedic are used with default params, not presented/evaluated as a release).
title: Comparison of semi-automatic and deep learning-based automatic methods for liver segmentation in living liver transplant donors
architecture_details: ITU_U-Net: initial 2D conv, 5 downsampling blocks (leaky ReLU, conv, BN), conv transpose upsampling with skip merges, 4x4 kernels/stride 2, SGD momentum 0.9, lr 0.0002, 300 epochs; METU_U-Net: U-Net with skip connections, BN before conv, PReLU, plus Conditional Adversarial Network (CAN) during training, 2D network using concatenated neighbor slices for 3D context; DEU_DeepMedic: 3D CNN + 3D fully connected CRF, default parameters; DEU_Nifty-Net: default parameters, TensorFlow; X_U-Net and Y_U-Net: U-Net with differing configurations/tuning. Ensemble fusion via majority voting (MV) and STAPLE.
loss_function: Not explicitly specified for U-Net variants; METU_U-Net adds a conditional adversarial (CAN) loss during training to regularize for sharper edge responses
preprocessing: ITU_U-Net: removal of intensities outside (-1500, 1500) HU, DICOM window level/width, histogram equalization explored (not used in final); METU_U-Net: per-image normalization; SLIVER07 data added to training set
postprocessing: METU_U-Net: 3D connected component analysis; ITU_U-Net: morphological post-processing explored but not used in final version
datasets: ["In-house living liver donor contrast-enhanced CT dataset (20 donors)", "SLIVER07 (added to training by ITU_U-Net)"]

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: 3D nnU-Net (3d_fullres) as primary method on volumetric abdominal CT for whole-liver segmentation, with quantitative evaluation (DSC, surface DSC 2mm, HD95, 2D Slice DSC) and statistical testing (Friedman/Dunn). title: Quality versus quantity of training datasets for artificial intelligence–based whole liver segmentation

postprocessing: None reported

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Deep learning (3D FCNN) is the primary method driving segmentation, refined by random walk post-processing; (2) explicitly uses 3D convolutions (3x3x3 kernels, volumetric sub-volumes 27^3/45^3) exploiting 3D spatial context; (3) segments the esophagus, an anatomical organ at risk; (4) CT-only modality; (5) reports quantitative metrics (DSC, ASSD, HD) with statistical testing; (6) novel contribution — authors claim first deep learning approach for esophagus segmentation and first CNN-driven random walker, achieving state-of-the-art on Synapse. Not a review, not tumor-only, not framework/tooling paper.
title: Esophagus segmentation in CT via 3D fully convolutional neural network and random walk
architecture: 3D Fully Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN) combined with Active Contour Model (ACM) and Random Walker (RW)
architecture_details: 13-layer 3D FCNN with dual re-scaled pathway (inspired by Kamnitsas et al. and Dolz et al.): 9 conv layers per path (25-75 kernels of 3x3x3), 3 fully-connected layers (400/200/150 units) converted to 1x1x1 convolutions, PReLU activations, unit strides; second pathway downsampled by factor 2 for larger receptive field; CNN probability map fitted with ACM centerline, then RW combines CNN, ACM distance map, and GMM-based HU intensity prior
loss_function: Cross-entropy averaged over all sub-volumes (softmax output)
preprocessing: CT voxels with HU < -150 and ACM distance map value <= 0.5 replaced with mean esophageal voxel intensity from training data (eliminates high gradients due to enclosed air); volumes split into sub-volumes (27x27x27 training, 45x45x45 testing)
postprocessing: Morphological closing operator applied to RW result to eliminate small false positive areas
datasets: ["Clinical dataset (University of Freiburg, EORTC 2211-08113 Lungtech protocol contours)", "Synapse multi-atlas dataset (MICCAI 2015 Multi-Atlas Labeling Beyond the Cranial Vault Workshop and Challenge)"]

screening_notes: Passes all criteria: 3D U-Net (deep learning, primary method) on 3D CT urography volumes; segments kidney (organ) plus renal tumor/cyst, so not tumor-only; DSC and AUC reported. Novelty is borderline (components are standard 3D U-Net), but the two-stage cascade (coarse global localization + fine high-res segmentation), multi-label tumor/cyst training, and VOI-based detection constitute a methodological contribution beyond plain application. Not a framework, review, or benchmark paper -> 'method'.
title: Automated segmentation of kidney and renal mass and automated detection of renal mass in CT urography using 3D U-Net-based deep convolutional neural network
architecture_details: Cascade of two 3D U-Nets for kidney (low-resolution global localization, then fine segmentation on cropped high-res localized images); single 3D U-Net for renal mass with multi-label learning (kidney/tumor/cyst trained simultaneously)
loss_function: Not reported
preprocessing: Separation of left/right kidneys via cropping; downsampling to low-resolution global images for localization; cropping and linear resampling of localized high-resolution images for fine segmentation
postprocessing: None explicitly reported; renal mass detection uses volume of maximum 3D VOI with a Youden-index-optimized threshold
datasets: ["In-house CTU cohort (Peking University First Hospital), corticomedullary phase", "In-house small renal tumor CTU cohort (external test only in spirit; same institution)"]

screening_notes: All 6 inclusion criteria met: (1) DL is primary method — novel 3D FCN (CENet); (2) fully volumetric, 3D convolutions, 128x128x64 volumes; (3) liver organ segmentation; (4) abdominal CT; (5) reports DSC, 95% HD, ASSD, sensitivity, precision with 8-fold cross-validation and t-tests; (6) novel contribution — adaptive contour self-supervision + residual shape branch + first cutout augmentation for segmentation. Not a review, not tumor-only, not 2D-only. Routing: method paper (no open-source framework/tooling presented).
title: Deeply self-supervised contour embedded neural network applied to liver segmentation
venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine
architecture: CENet — 3D fully convolutional V-net-based encoder-decoder with densely connected blocks
architecture_details: V-net-style contracting/expanding paths with D_Block modules (DenseNet-style dense connections using depth-wise separable convolutions, k=16, n=4); two deeply supervised branches: contour transition (adaptive self-supervision erasing already-correct contour voxels via decaying threshold p: 1.0→0.5) and shape transition (two complementary extractors combined by subtraction, i.e., residual shape estimation); features merged by out-transition layers
loss_function: Dice loss (main output and shape branch) + softmax cross-entropy with class-balancing weights (contour branch) + L2 regularization; weights α=1, β=1, γ=0.1
preprocessing: Resampling to 128x128x64; intensity windowing level=10, width=700 (clip [-340, 360]); normalization to [0,1]; on-the-fly random affine deformation (80% probability); cutout augmentation with random zero mask 5L≤l≤4L (80% probability)
postprocessing: None for segmentation (curvature flow smoothing applied only for surface visualization)
datasets: ["Public abdominal CT dataset from Gibson et al. (DenseVNet, zenodo.1169361)", "MICCAI SLiVer07", "3Dircadb", "Private clinically annotated dataset"]
dataset_size: 160 abdominal CT scans (90 + 20 + 20 + 30); 8-fold CV: 140 train / 20 validation
comparison_methods: ["DSN (3D deeply supervised network, Dou et al.)", "VoxResNet", "DenseVNet", "CENet ablations (CENet-A, CENet-C, CENet-S, CENet-R)"]
training_time: 10 hours (300 epochs, Adam, batch size 4, lr 0.001)
limitations: Portal vein entry region segmented poorly by all methods due to inconsistent ground-truth annotations (clinicians disagreed on vessel inclusion); dense block parameters (k, n) and contour threshold p require retuning for other applications; only single-organ (liver) evaluation
future_work: Concurrent and integrated liver + vascular system segmentation framework to overcome annotation variability

screening_notes: Meets DL (V-Net FCN), 3D (volumetric V-Net), CT (Task06_Lung/TCIA), organ (lung parenchyma, 98% DSC, in addition to tumor), and quantitative evaluation (DSC) criteria. screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Deep learning is the primary method (novel DAB-CNN combining attention gates, channel boosting, and deep supervision); (2) fully 3D/volumetric processing (128x128x64 voxel inputs, 3x3x3 kernels, 3D cascaded CNN); (3) segments pelvic organs at risk (prostate, bladder, rectum, penile bulb); (4) uses planning CT scans from 120 prostate radiotherapy patients; (5) reports quantitative Dice and average surface distance (ASD) metrics with statistical significance tests; (6) novel contribution - authors claim first implementation of attention gates combined with channel boosting for semantic CT segmentation. No exclusion criteria apply. Not a framework paper - it is a novel segmentation method, so study type is 'method' and framework-specific fields (F1-F3) are not applicable.
title: Attention-enabled 3D boosted convolutional neural networks for semantic CT segmentation using deep supervision
architecture: DAB-CNN: deeply supervised attention-enabled boosted convolutional neural network (3D fully-convolutional cascaded CNN)
architecture_details: 4 multi-scale level 3D cascaded encoder-decoder with 3x3x3 kernels, residual connections per level, additive spatial attention gates (sigmoidal, vector-concatenation based) on skip connections, deep supervision via learned deconvolutional upsampling with decaying multi-scale loss weights (initialized 0.25, decayed 0.0005/0.001/0.005), and incremental channel boosting with a base network plus 2 boosted networks (50% and 25% channels) trained via sequestered learning with locked base parameters; batch normalization, PReLU, and 0.3 dropout; auxiliary simplified U-Net for center-of-mass localization
loss_function: Soft Dice loss (differentiable) with 1e-6 stabilization term; multi-channel soft Dice for base/1st boosted networks, single-structure soft Dice for 2nd boosted network; deep supervision with dynamically weighted and decayed multi-scale soft Dice losses
preprocessing: Resampling to 0.98mm x 0.98mm x 3mm, intensity normalization, on-the-fly augmentation (non-rigid deformations, rotations, translational shifts, resolution variations, synthetic metal/fiducial artifact contamination, noise contamination)
postprocessing: Predictions resampled back to original resolution for final evaluation
datasets: ["Institutional prostate cancer planning CT dataset (Siemens scanner, 120 kVp, single-observer MIM Maestro contours)"]
dataset_size: 120 patients (80 training, 20 internal validation, 20 hold-out test; Kaggle-style rules with test set used once)
other_metrics: {"ASD_mm_prostate": 0.78, "ASD_mm_bladder": 0.88, "ASD_mm_rectum": 1.11, "ASD_mm_penile_bulb": 1.27, "statistical_tests": "Two-sample one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests; DAB-CNN significantly superior (p<0.05) to DA-UNet, ResNeXt, LL-CNN, B-UNet, D-UNet, A-UNet, UNet on prostate, rectum, penile bulb Dice (bladder vs DA-UNet not significant, p=0.086)"}
comparison_methods: ["UNet (variation)", "A-UNet (attention U-Net)", "B-UNet (boosted U-Net)", "D-UNet (deeply-supervised U-Net)", "ResNeXt (U-Net with ResNeXt blocks)", "LL-CNN (life-long learning segmentation CNN)", "DA-UNet (deeply supervised attention U-Net)"]
training_time: ~28 hours for all 4 OARs (DAB-CNN); comparators: UNet ~20h, A-UNet ~24h, D-UNet ~16h, B-UNet ~32h, DA-UNet ~16h
inference_time: ~6 seconds for all 4 OARs (DAB-CNN); comparators ~6-7 seconds
limitations: Algorithm struggles in presence of heavy metal artifacts (fiducial markers) despite synthetic artifact augmentation; simple structures like bladder may not require sophisticated models; clinical significance of improved contour accuracy unclear; dataset quality limited by manual delineation variability (single observer used for consistency); GPU memory constraints limit 3D network size; boosted networks cannot make meaningful predictions without the base network
future_work: A planned future study will evaluate the dosimetric impact of segmentation accuracy

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: deep learning (cascaded modified U-Net) as primary method, CT (LiTS), liver organ segmentation (plus tumor), quantitative Dice reported (0.95 liver / 0.69 tumor), and a modest novel contribution (decoder modified to keep feature count constant during up-convolution; cascade of two U-Nets). Caveats: (1) title claims 3D and evaluation is volumetric, but explicit 3D convolutions are never described — architecture reads like 2D U-Net on slices; flagged is_3d=true per title/volumetric claims with low certainty. (2) Tumor Dice inconsistent within paper (0.69 abstract/table vs 0.65 results text; conclusion says liver 0.96 vs 0.95 elsewhere). Tumor-only would trigger exclusion rule 5, but liver is segmented, so rule does not apply.
title: CT Guided Diagnosis: Cascaded U-Net for 3D Segmentation of Liver and Tumor
venue: IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering (IConACES 2020)
architecture_details: First U-Net takes raw CT input and outputs a liver probability map; probability map + original image feed the second U-Net which segments liver and tumor. Decoder modified vs. original U-Net (Ronneberger et al.): up-convolution keeps the same number of features as the previous layer instead of halving, to reduce information loss; encoder features concatenated after up-sampling.
loss_function: Categorical cross-entropy
preprocessing: Windowing / window clipping at [-100, 400] HU for contrast enhancement
postprocessing: None mentioned
dataset_size: 130 LiTS subjects used; trained and tested with 8 held-out subjects for evaluation (LiTS contains 201 CTs, 131 with ground truth)
comparison_methods: ["ResNet (Bi et al., cascaded deep residual)", "H-DenseUNet", "nnU-Net", "DeepX (Yuan, hierarchical conv-deconv)", "Cascaded ResNet"]
limitations: Class imbalance (tumor vs non-tumor) degrades tumor segmentation accuracy; false negatives occur in tumor segmentation (e.g., central tumor regions); tumor Dice limited (0.69) compared to liver (0.95).
future_work: Further modification/investigation required for tumor segmentation; architecture may be changed with different connectivity for better results.

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: DL-primary (modified SharpMask FCN, two-stage hierarchical), thoracic CT volumes with 3D context (z-extent ROI selection, 3D B-spline deformation augmentation), organs at risk (esophagus + heart/trachea/aorta), quantitative Dice (0.72±0.07), novel contribution (hierarchical two-stage design, transposed-conv refinement, Dice loss). title: Fully automated esophagus segmentation with a hierarchical deep learning approach
venue: IEEE International Conference on Signal and Image Processing Applications (ICSIPA 2017)
architecture: Hierarchical two-stage Fully Convolutional Network based on SharpMask
architecture_details: Stage 1: modified SharpMask for multi-organ segmentation (transposed convolutions instead of bilinear upsampling in refinement module; conv+ReLU on skip connections to equalize channel counts; 7x7 kernels). Stage 2: second SharpMask fine-tuned on 128x128 esophagus-centered ROI using stage-1 probability maps of neighboring organs (auto-context-like); slices with <10 connected voxels excluded from z-range.
loss_function: Dice Loss (as introduced in V-Net)
preprocessing: Intensity normalization to zero mean/unit variance; body contour used to exclude background during training
postprocessing: Connected-component filter on stage-1 output (>10 voxels per slice) to derive the esophagus ROI/z-range for stage 2; no other postprocessing reported
datasets: ["Private thoracic CT dataset (30 scans; lung cancer or Hodgkin lymphoma patients with manual delineations)"]
dataset_size: 30 CT scans (6-fold CV: 25 train / 5 test per fold)
comparison_methods: ["OPAL (Optimized PatchMatch label fusion, atlas-based)", "SharpMask single-stage (Step 1)", "SharpMask + CRFasRNN"]
limitations: Small dataset (30 scans); esophagus Dice of 0.72 leaves room for improvement given low CT contrast; baseline SharpMask stage still has false negatives requiring the second stage
future_work: Investigating new ways to incorporate spatial context, such as auto-context models

screening_notes: Passes all six include criteria: primary DL method (V-Net variant with multi-rate dilated bottleneck DDN and novel Weighted Fusion Loss), true 3D volumetric processing (Conv3d, 128x128x64 voxel volumes), pancreas organ segmentation, CT (TCIA CT-82, contrast-enhanced), quantitative metrics (Dice 0.833, sensitivity 0.877, precision 0.970), and methodological novelty (DDN module + WFL loss). title: Deep Dilated V-Net for 3D Volume Segmentation of Pancreas in CT images
venue: 2020 7th International Conference on Signal Processing and Integrated Networks (SPIN)
architecture_details: Deep Dilated V-Net (DDV-Net): multi-rate Deep Dilated Network (rates 1, 3, 5) with channel-wise feature excitation (adaptive average pooling + 1x1x1 conv) inserted at the V-Net bottleneck; ELU activations; 2x2x2 stride-2 convolutions instead of max-pooling; residual and encoder-decoder skip connections; dropout at high-level layers; Kaiming initialization
loss_function: Weighted Fusion Loss (WFL) = alpha * BBCE + (1 - alpha) * SDC; Balanced Binary Cross-Entropy (beta=0.23) + Smooth Dice Coefficient loss; alpha=0.2 after tuning
preprocessing: Per-sample intensity normalization to [0,1] (mean subtraction, std division); random flip augmentation; axial resizing; clipping of third dimension near pancreas centroid to fixed 128x128x64 voxels at 1x1x1.5 mm resolution
postprocessing: None reported

comparison_methods: ["V-Net", "Attention U-Net", "U-Net"]
limitations: No explicit limitations section; implied: single small dataset (82 scans), single organ; best model only trained once on fixed train/val split

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) deep learning is the primary method (2-D CNN for VOI localization + 3-D residual CNN for segmentation); (2) true 3-D processing with volumetric 5x5x5 kernels on 128x128x64 VOIs, explicitly contrasted with 2-D slice-wise methods; (3) segments the prostate, an anatomical organ; (4) CT modality (150 CT scans from two hospitals); (5) quantitative evaluation via DSC/SEN/PPV with five-fold cross-validation; (6) methodological contribution in the CNN-based VOI extraction method (CBVEM) plus a deeper residual 3-D CNN vs. V-Net. title: Automatic Segmentation of the Prostate on 3D CT Images by Using Multiple Deep Learning Networks
venue: ICBBE '18 (ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedical Engineering), Okinawa, Japan
architecture: Two-stage pipeline: 2-D U-Net-like CNN for VOI localization (CBVEM) followed by a 3-D residual encoder-decoder CNN for prostate segmentation
architecture_details: 3-D CNN in V-Net-like contracting/expanding structure where convolutions are replaced by residual units (each with three 5x5x5 conv layers, per He et al.); 2x2x2 down-convolutions and deconvolutions for resolution changes; final 1x1x1 conv with voxel-wise softmax into foreground/background probability maps. 2-D CNN uses 3x3 kernels with skip connections for prostate center-point localization.
loss_function: Differentiable Dice similarity coefficient (Dice loss, V-Net style); explicit gradient formulation provided
preprocessing: Resample pixel size to 1.0 mm in x,y,z; intensity thresholding at 250 to detect bone structures (coccyx, symphysis pubis) for coarse prostate-region slice identification; CNN-based VOI extraction to fixed 128x128x64 voxels at 1x1x1 mm; massive data augmentation (20-degree rotation, 10-voxel translation, horizontal flips, B-spline dense deformation field on a 2x2x2 control-point grid)
postprocessing: None beyond binarization of the softmax probability map at threshold > 0.5
datasets: ["Private dataset from Ruijin Hospital of Shanghai Jiaotong University and Xuhui Central Hospital, Shanghai"]
dataset_size: 150 CT scans (expert manually delineated); ~3000+ augmented images per fold
comparison_methods: ["Atlas/registration-based method of Han et al. (SPIE 2015): 81.31% DSC on the same 150 patients", "Deep learning + multi-atlas fusion of Ma et al. (2017): 86.80% DSC on 92 patients", "Internal ablation: same 3-D CNN trained without CBVEM"]

inference_time: Not quantified; only claimed faster than atlas-based, deformable model-based, and feature-based methods

screening_notes: DL is primary method (FCN-DecNet built on VGG-16) for liver/spleen/kidney segmentation on abdominal CT with quantitative Dice/Precision/Recall/IU evaluation and clear architectural novelty (new unpooling layer, fusion layers, MS-PA optimization). Borderline on criterion 2: the FCN itself processes 2D 512x512 slices (is_3d=false, no 3D convolutions), but the full pipeline is not purely 2D-independent — the MS-PA optimization uses volumetric nonlinear registration (affine + B-spline), cross-slice voxel neighborhoods (9x9 in previous/next slices), and 3D organ reconstruction, so exclusion criterion 3 ('2D without 3D context') is not triggered. Included with moderate confidence; flag for reviewer if strict '3D convolutions required' interpretation is used.
title: A Multiorgan Segmentation Model for CT Volumes via Full Convolution-Deconvolution Network
architecture: FCN-DecNet (full convolution-deconvolution network initialized from VGG-16)
architecture_details: VGG-16 backbone with fully connected layers converted to convolutions; 1x1 conv predicting 4 classes (liver, spleen, kidney, background); 4 rounds of upsampling with a new unpooling layer (fills with mean of whole feature map instead of zeros), deconvolutional layers, and fusion layers combining predictions from pool3/pool4/pool5 and fc7; final output at stride 8. Coarse FCN output refined by multiscale weights probabilistic atlas (MS-PA) with image-wise (PCC), organ-wise (Jaccard*PCC), and voxel-wise (normalized Euclidean intensity distance) weights and Bayes-based estimation.
loss_function: Not reported
preprocessing: CT volumes divided into fixed-size 512x512 slices for FCN-DecNet training; atlas images aligned via nonlinear registration (affine transformation + B-spline transformation) for MS-PA construction
postprocessing: FCN-DecNet coarse segmentation refined by MS-PA via Bayes-based estimation (mean of voxel probabilities from FCN-DecNet and MS-PA, max-mean label assignment); pixel probabilities stacked into voxel probabilities; 3D organs reconstructed from slice sequence

screening_notes: Borderline case. Satisfies 3D (3D convolutions), CT modality, quantitative metrics (DSC, MSD, 95% HD), and novelty criteria. However, DL plays only an auxiliary role: a 3D U-Net (essentially Çiçek et al. with minor modifications, e.g., strided convolutions) segments only the bladder to steer the registration cost function, and a 2D GAN inpaints rectal gas pockets. Reported DSC/MSD/HD results for prostate, SV, LN, rectum measure registration quality, not DL segmentation performance. Given the review focus on 3D organ segmentation using deep learning as the primary method, this is excluded despite the DL component.
exclusion_reason: Deep learning is not the primary segmentation method (Exclusion Criterion 2). The paper's core contribution is a deformable image registration pipeline (elastix, B-spline, multi-stage) for contour propagation in adaptive proton therapy; organ contours (prostate, seminal vesicles, lymph nodes, rectum, bladder) are produced by registration propagation, not by a deep network.

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: primary method is 3D CNN (DenseNet-based shape autoencoder + SC-SegNet, all 3D operations); processes 3D CT volumes with 3D context; segments liver (organ); CT modality (Sliver07, CHAOS); reports Dice, VOE, ASSD, RMSD, MSSD, challenge scores; novel contribution via hybrid loss (adaptively weighted CE, edge-preserving smoothness, shape constraint). title: Automatic liver segmentation using 3D convolutional neural networks with a hybrid loss function
architecture: SC-SegNet (shape-constrained densely connected segmentation network) cascaded with a 3D DenseNet-based liver shape autoencoder

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Deep learning is the primary method (V-net-based CNN + 3D CRF-RNN); (2) Fully 3D/volumetric processing - all layers implemented in 3D, volumes resampled to 128x128x64; (3) Segments an anatomical organ (bladder); (4) CT modality; (5) Quantitative metrics reported (DSC 92.24%, VOE, RVD, ASD, MSD); (6) Novel contributions: first application of 3D fully connected CRF-RNN in medical image processing, novel dual-channel preprocessing, end-to-end joint training of CNN+CRF outperforming offline CRF post-processing. title: Automatic bladder segmentation from CT images using deep CNN and 3D fully connected CRF-RNN
venue: International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery

postprocessing: 3D fully connected CRF-RNN refinement integrated as part of the network (jointly trained, not offline post-processing); compared against and outperforms offline 3D CRF post-processing
datasets: ["Private clinical dataset (single hospital, multiple CT scanners)"]
dataset_size: 124 CT volumes (100 training / 24 validation); slices 256x256 or 512x512; 65-156 slices per volume
comparison_methods: ["V-net (reimplemented)", "V-net with dual-channel preprocessing", "V-net + batch normalization (their CNN)", "Dual-channel preprocessing + their CNN", "Their CNN + 3D CRF-RNN (ablation)", "Their CNN + 3D fully connected CRF as offline post-processing (ablation)"]
gpu_used: NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti (11 GB); Intel Core i7-5960X CPU at 3.00 GHz
training_time: Not explicitly stated; two-stage training: 400 epochs CNN-only (lr=1e-4, batch=2) then 10 epochs fine-tuning with 3D CRF-RNN (lr=1e-7, batch=1); SGD, weight decay 0.0005, momentum 0.99
inference_time: 5.4 s per CT volume (vs. 0.9 s for V-net baseline)
limitations: False positive regions around bladder caused by soft-tissues/tumors with similar density that mislead the CRF long-range connections (and are amplified by dual-channel preprocessing); reported results may be over-fitted to validation set since no held-out test set was used; limited GPU memory restricts input size and batch size; average segmentation time (5.4 s) higher than baseline V-net (0.9 s)
future_work: Distinguish soft-tissues/tumors with appearance similar to bladder; collect more images and build a dedicated unseen test set; extend approach to other organs (liver, pancreas); investigate other modalities such as MRI
