limitations: Undersegmentation of tumors at the liver boundary (DSC drops to 0.923 in worst case, RVD -11.166); preprocessing can amplify intra-liver intensity variation and occasionally removes small liver tissue at boundaries (5/60 cases); vessel parts may be wrongly included by axial cavity filling; model size restricted by GPU memory; performance on unseen data (VISCERAL) is slightly weaker than methods trained on that data; evaluated only on relatively small datasets
future_work: Test on CT volumes from multiple data sources to analyze weaknesses and enable integration into real-life applications; improve the 3D CNN model to further integrate top-down information into the network for more robust performance on heterogeneous data

screening_notes: 3D CNN (11-layer, 3D convolutions) is the primary method for liver detection/probability map generation, refined by a globally optimized surface evolution model — deep learning is central, not incidental. Processes 3D CT volumes (512×512×~279). Segments liver (an organ) from abdominal CT. Quantitative evaluation: Dice 97.25±0.65% on Sliver07-II online testing, Sliver07 score 80.3±4.5, VOE/RVD/ASD/RMSD/MSD reported, plus comparisons against 7 state-of-the-art methods and the 3D CNN-GC baseline. Novel contribution: new energy functional with adaptive global/local prior data term and convex max-flow global optimization. Meets all inclusion criteria.
title: Automatic 3D liver segmentation based on deep learning and globally optimized surface evolution
architecture_details: Eleven-layer 3D CNN with PReLU activations, two average pooling layers, three Doublesize layers, and logistic regression output; network spread across 4 GPUs (Krizhevsky-style parallelization) from Conv3 to Conv7. CNN output probability map is thresholded (t=0.5) to yield initial segmentation and shape prior; refinement via energy functional (region statistics + shape prior + weighted total variation) minimized by continuous max-flow convex optimization (Yuan et al.) for global surface evolution
loss_function: Cross-entropy with weight decay (CNN training); variational energy functional with data, shape-prior, and boundary regularization terms (refinement)
preprocessing: All images adjusted to 279 slices by appending/deleting non-liver slices; cropped to 496×496×279 input blocks from 512×512×279 volumes; refinement stage downsampled to 256×256 per slice
postprocessing: Morphological closing and cavity filling; intrahepatic vessels enclosed by liver tissue included
dataset_size: 151 CT volumes total (30 Sliver07: 20 with ground truth + 10 online testing; 121 local hospital); 109 for CNN training, 42 for testing
comparison_methods: ["Kainmüller et al 2007", "Wimmer et al 2009", "Linguraru et al 2012", "Al-Shaikhli et al 2015", "Dong et al 2015", "Lu et al 2015 (3D CNN-GC)", "Gauriau et al 2013"]
framework: cuda-convnet (CNN); MATLAB 2014b; GPU max-flow code of Yuan et al.
inference_time: ~135 s per volume (3 s CNN testing, 105 s data-term computation, 25 s continuous max-flow, 2 s other)
limitations: Not explicitly stated in available text; parameters (α1, α2, λ, γ, threshold t) empirically set, though sensitivity analysis shows relative stability in wide ranges. Method is liver-specific (fixed input sizing to 279 slices)
future_work: Not stated in available text (paper content truncated after section 5.3)

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: (1) primary method is a 3D deeply supervised fully convolutional network; (2) true volumetric processing (3×3×3 convolutions, 3D CAFFE, 96×96×96 volumes); (3) segments six torso organs (heart, lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys); (4) micro-CT is a CT modality — note this is preclinical mouse imaging, not human clinical CT, which may be worth flagging depending on review scope; (5) reports Dice, recovery coefficient, precision, recall; (6) novel contribution via two-stage rough-to-fine architecture, deep supervision for anatomical priors, and pseudo low-contrast training data generation. Exclusion checks: not a review, DL is primary, 3D context, CT modality, organs not tumors, quantitative metrics present, methodological contribution present.
title: Prediction of major torso organs in low-contrast micro-CT images of mice using a two-stage deeply supervised fully convolutional network
architecture: Two-stage deeply supervised fully convolutional network (TS-DSN)
architecture_details: 3D FCN with 12 layers, 3×3×3 kernels, stride-2 downsampling, batch norm + ReLU; auxiliary deconvolutional branches provide deep supervision of intermediate layers using ground-truth labels as anatomical priors. Stage 1: global multi-organ network on whole torso; Stage 2: six organ-specific local networks on bounding-box crops from stage-1 predictions.
loss_function: Softmax cross-entropy (main + auxiliary deep supervision losses weighted by α_u, decayed 5%/10 epochs from 0.3/0.4) plus L2 regularization
preprocessing: Pseudo low-contrast images generated from contrast-enhanced micro-CT by subtracting intensity offset μ∈(200,800) within expert-labeled liver/spleen/kidney regions; torso cropping; resampling to 96×96×96; grayscale normalization to [0,1]; data augmentation by voxel shifts (0, ±1, ±3, ±5 per axis)
postprocessing: Threshold 0.01 on probability maps for binary labels; largest connected component extraction per organ for 3D bounding-box cropping (stage-2 input)
dataset_size: 40 contrast-enhanced micro-CT images (5-fold-style cross-validation: 35 train / 5 test, 8 repeats) + 10 real low-contrast micro-CT images (qualitative testing)
other_metrics: {"recovery_coefficient": "reported as box plots (TS-DSN closest to 1)", "precision": "reported as box plots (TS-DSN higher than FCN/DSN)", "recall": "reported as box plots (moderate; exact values not in text)", "dice_improvements_vs_SSM": "+18% left kidney, +26% spleen"}
comparison_methods: ["FCN (Shelhamer et al., no deep supervision)", "3D DSN (Dou et al., deep supervision without two-stage)", "SSM statistical shape model atlas registration (Wang et al. 2012b)", "Dense V-net (Gibson et al. 2018)"]
gpu_used: 3× NVIDIA P40 GPUs (128 GB RAM server)
training_time: ~30 hours per training session; 30000 iterations, SGD (lr 0.01, poly decay power 0.9, weight decay 0.005, momentum 0.9, batch size 1)
limitations: Real low-contrast image results less accurate than pseudo low-contrast results (though predictions mostly lie inside target organs); generalizability concern across scanners, acquisition protocols, animal sizes, and body postures; training parameters empirically tuned for this specific low-contrast micro-CT data.
future_work: Enlarge training set to improve generalizability; simulate varied pseudo training images using deformable mouse phantom or MOBY phantom with different scanner configurations; alternatively acquire paired non-contrast/contrast-enhanced scans of the same subject with non-rigid registration for label transfer; investigate more advanced methods of incorporating anatomical priors.

screening_notes: Meets all 6 include criteria: (1) DL primary method — custom 3D CNN (MCE + light 3D ResU-Net); (2) true 3D volumetric processing with 3D convolutions; (3) organ segmentation (spleen, liver); (4) both datasets are CT (private spleen CT + LiTS liver CT); (5) quantitative metrics (Dice, VOE, Jaccard, inference time); (6) novel contribution (new 3D multiple-contextual extractor module and light 3D ResU-Net architecture). Routed as 'method' — not a framework paper (no open-source tooling/release). Caveat: organ coverage is one organ per dataset/model (spleen OR liver), not simultaneous multi-organ segmentation; multi_organ flagged false accordingly.
title: An Efficient and Accurate 3D Multiple-Contextual Semantic Segmentation Network for Medical Volumetric Images
venue: 2021 43rd Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine & Biology Society (EMBC)
architecture_details: Asymmetric unified 3D network. MCE extracts low/high-level contextual features (Fc1, Fc2), aligns resolutions via trilinear interpolation, fuses them by two concatenation-conv steps (Fs1 = conv([Fc1,Fc2]), Fs2 = conv([Fc1,Fs1])) with fixed 36 channels. Backbone is 3D residual blocks (3x3x3 kernels, Conv3D + InstanceNorm + ReLU) forming a light 3D ResU-Net with downsampling and concat-based upsampling path.
loss_function: Dice loss (with smoothness term sigma, minimized via derived gradient)
preprocessing: HU intensity truncation to [200, 250] HU as printed in paper (likely [-200, 250]); resampling to 2.0x2.0x2.0 mm3 (spleen) and 2.0x2.0x5.0 mm3 (liver); intensity normalization to [0, 1] for training/testing; random weight initialization
postprocessing: None — predictions made directly from single-model training/testing 'without relying on any post processing tools'
datasets: ["Private spleen dataset (Shiga University of Medical Science Hospital)", "LiTS (MICCAI 2017 Liver Tumor Segmentation Challenge)"]
dataset_size: 181 CT scans total: 50 spleen (41 train / 9 test) + 131 liver (103 train / 28 test)
comparison_methods: ["3D U-Net", "V-Net", "VoxResNet", "3D DSD-FCN", "MultiResUNet"]
inference_time: ~0.52 s per full 3D volume (spleen: 0.518 s; liver: 0.526 s) vs 2.5-5.5 s for compared methods
limitations: Paper states 'Some limitations are presented to optimize future work' but does not enumerate them in the provided text. Implicit limitations: small private spleen dataset (50 scans), only two organs evaluated (one per model/dataset), no code release.
future_work: Authors believe the network can be applied to other medical image segmentation tasks; limitations to be addressed in future work (not detailed).

screening_notes: Meets all criteria: DL primary (ResUNet with novel DCE loss); CT volumes (LiTS); liver organ segmentation; quantitative Dice reported; novel contributions (DCE loss, 3D_CRF + 3D_CCA post-processing pipeline). 3D criterion satisfied via 5-slice multi-image input plus 3D post-processing, though the network itself uses 2D convolutions (no 3D convs). Single-organ (liver), which is fine per criteria. Study type: method (novel architecture variant + loss + post-processing pipeline, not a framework/benchmark/review).
title: Liver Segmentation in CT based on ResUNet with 3D Probabilistic and Geometric Post Process
venue: IEEE 4th International Conference on Signal and Image Processing (ICSIP)
architecture: ResUNet (U-Net with residual units and batch normalization)
architecture_details: 5 downsampling/upsampling blocks (vs 3 in baseline [11]), 3x3 convolutions, multi-image input of 5 consecutive CT slices as input channels for context; deep supervision-free encoder-decoder with pooling/un-pooling
loss_function: Proposed DCE loss: linear combination of Dice loss and weighted Cross-Entropy, DCE = 0.5*Dice + 0.5*CE (epsilon=0.5; CE class weights: background 0.2, liver 1.2)
preprocessing: Hounsfield unit clipping to [-200, 200] HU; histogram equalization for contrast enhancement
postprocessing: Fully connected 3D conditional random field (3D_CRF, two Gaussian kernels over position/HU, Krähenbühl fast inference); 3D connected component analysis (3D_CCA) keeping 3 largest components via union-find
dataset_size: Train: 130 CT scans / 91 patients (50,622 images); Test: 70 CT scans / 40 patients (26,608 images); ~35% of slices contain liver
comparison_methods: ["ResUNet + CrossEntropy loss (0.906)", "ResUNet + Dice loss (0.918)", "ResUNet_DCE + 2D_CRF (0.943)", "H-DenseUNet (Li et al., 0.960)", "Han et al. residual 3-class U-Net (0.961)"]
training_time: Not reported (DCE converges at ~200k iterations vs ~400k for CE alone)
limitations: Not explicitly stated; tumor segmentation not addressed (deferred to future work); evaluation limited to LiTS liver class; best Dice (0.960) matches rather than exceeds Li et al. and is slightly below Han et al. (0.961)
future_work: Extend methods to liver tumor segmentation and evaluate on more CT scans from hospitals

screening_notes: Meets all inclusion criteria: DL primary method (3D U-Net + ResNet-50), full 3D volumetric processing with multi-resolution coarse/fine VOI pipeline, segments 4 OARs (esophagus, heart, trachea, aorta) on CT (SegTHOR, 60 scans), reports Dice and Hausdorff. Novelty is borderline (modified U-Net variant + two-stage inference; results do not outperform SegTHOR top participants), but architectural modifications (ResNet-50 encoder, up-sampling layers, loss weighting) and the coarse-to-fine pipeline constitute a methodological contribution sufficient for criterion 6; not a mere application of off-the-shelf methods. Exclusion criterion 7 not triggered.
title: Segmentation of Organs at Risk in Chest Cavity Using 3D Deep Neural Network
venue: IEEE Signal Processing Society conference (IEEE Xplore)
architecture: 3D U-Net with ResNet-50 backbone (two-stage multi-resolution: coarse-resolution localization network + fine-resolution segmentation network)
architecture_details: Vanilla encoder replaced by ResNet-50; shortcut connections between encoder/decoder after each downsampling; batch norm before all activations; transposed convolutions replaced by 3D up-sampling layers; softmax output; 5-fold cross-validation with ensemble of 5 models at inference; crops fixed at 64x128x128, fine-stage VOI crop 256^3
loss_function: Generalized Dice Loss (with empirically computed class weights from 200 generated samples)
preprocessing: HU clipping to [-1200, 600] and normalization to [0,1]; coarse-resolution data resampled to 6x6x6 mm per voxel; esophagus and trachea masks dilated by 10 mm in coarse stage to prevent label diminishing; equalization/resampling/augmentation tested but did not outperform normalization only
postprocessing: Keep largest 3D connected component for heart, trachea, aorta; keep connected components >500 voxels for esophagus (tubular shape); only positive predictions per organ VOI considered
datasets: ["SegTHOR 2019 (expanded with 30-CT dataset from Trullo et al.)"]
dataset_size: 60 thoracic CT scans (40 train/validation, 20 test); 0.98x0.98x(2-3.7) mm resolution
comparison_methods: ["Miaofei Han et al. (multi-resolution VB-nets)", "Tao He et al. (multi-task learning)", "Qin Wang et al. (3D enhanced multi-scale network)", "Pan Chen et al. (two-stage network)"]
training_time: Not mentioned (RMSprop, lr 1e-3 /10 every 30 epochs, batch size 4, 100 epochs x 100 iterations, 5-fold CV)
inference_time: 20-25 seconds per CT image (ensemble of 5 models)
limitations: Results comparable to but do not outperform SegTHOR top participants (e.g., esophagus Dice 0.77 vs 0.865 best); esophagus segmentation remains challenging due to variable shape/position and low contrast
future_work: Improve model architecture and system pipeline to outperform existing approaches in both performance and speed

screening_notes: Passes DL focus (U-Net + residual modules, PyTorch), CT modality, quantitative metrics (Dice 0.87, IoU 0.77, Hausdorff 4.36mm), and segments an anatomical structure (left atrium). Fails 3D criterion decisively: paper states the model 'accepts two-dimensional axial CT image sections as input' and the volume segmentation is produced by feeding 'each axial section of the volume sequentially into the model' then concatenating 2D maps along z — slice-independent processing with no 3D context. Secondary concern: the methodological contribution is minimal (standard U-Net with residual modules and instance normalization; no hyperparameter search), as the paper's primary novelty is the clinical finding (LA volume as AF biomarker), which also weakly triggers the 'applies existing methods without methodological contribution' criterion.
exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context

screening_notes: Deep learning is the primary method (RefineNet, U-Net, FCN, CE-Net, UNet3D, ResUNet3D). Includes genuinely 3D processing via newly developed RefineNetPlus3D (all 2D ops replaced with 3D counterparts). Segments multiple anatomical organs at risk (bladder, small intestine, rectum, femoral heads) plus CTV on contrast-enhanced CT. Reports DSC, Jaccard, ASSD. Novel contribution: adapted 2D RefineNet and new RefineNetPlus3D architecture with 3D Refine block. No exclusion criteria met.
title: RefineNet-based 2D and 3D automatic segmentations for clinical target volume and organs at risks for patients with cervical cancer in postoperative radiotherapy
venue: Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics
architecture_details: 2D RefineNet: ResNet50 encoder + decoder with residual convolutional unit (RCU), chained residual pooling (CRP), and fusion. RefineNetPlus3D: all 2D operations replaced with 3D counterparts, 3D Refine block with added ReLU activations and batch normalization, first down/up-sampling layer modified to rate 1/2, shortcut connections from encoder to decoder. Baselines: FCN, U-Net, CE-Net, UNet3D, ResUNet3D.
loss_function: Dice-coefficient loss (2D models); binary cross-entropy loss ('binary gross-entropy' as printed) (3D models); Adam optimizer
preprocessing: CT simulation iliac crest to ischial tuberosities, 3-mm slice thickness, intravenous contrast, DICOM, 512x512 matrix; data augmentation with random rotation
postprocessing: None reported
datasets: ["Institutional retrospective dataset (Wenzhou Medical University First Affiliated Hospital), cervical cancer postoperative radiotherapy CT"]
dataset_size: 313 patients (44,222 CT slices): 251 training / 31 validation / 31 testing
organs_segmented: ["clinical target volume (CTV)", "bladder", "small intestine", "rectum", "right femoral head", "left femoral head"]
comparison_methods: ["FCN", "U-Net", "CE-Net", "UNet3D", "ResUNet3D", "(literature) Dense V-Net", "(literature) CNN (Rhee et al.)", "(literature) 3D CNN (Wang et al.)", "(literature) DpnU-Net (Liu et al.)"]
training_time: Not reported (poly LR schedule: 2e-4 for 2D, 1e-4 for 3D models; batch size 6 for 2D, 2 for 3D)
inference_time: ~6.4 s CTV / ~6.6 s OARs (RefineNetPlus3D); ~3.2-3.9 s (2D RefineNet); manual contouring baseline 90-120 min per patient
limitations: CTV DSC (0.82) lower than ~0.86 reported by other groups (Rhee et al., Wang et al., Liu et al.), indicating room for improvement; poorer rectum segmentation attributed to small volume and unclear outlines; image and manual contour quality may affect accuracy and need further investigation; single-institution, single-vendor (Philips) contrast-enhanced CT cohort.
future_work: Further investigation of factors affecting contouring accuracy, such as image and manual contour quality
